messages.body_plain:
I read that as g[j] < s[j] < 1 rather than g[j] + s[j] < 1.
You can still use a simplex, but now you don't need to add
and can just have:

>   g <- to_vector(theta[, 1]);

>   s <- to_vector(theta[, 2]);

You can add whatever prior you like on top of the implicit
uniform over values meeting the constraint that 0 < g[j] + s[j] < 1.

But if you try to write

> g[j]~beta(a_g,b_g) and s[j]~beta(a_s,b_s)

and mean the joint prior to be

 p(g[j], s[j] | a_g, b_g, a_s, b_s)

 = beta(g[j] | a_g, b_g) * beta(s[j] | a_s, b_s)

you have a problem because it doesn't integrate to 1 over the
values of g and s meeting the constraint that 0 < g + s < 1.
If a and b are constants, it'll only be off by a constant, but
if they are parameters, you have to figure out how to account
for them, like taking the second distribution over s to be
truncated.  That is, take the prior to be

 p(g[j], s[j] | a_g, b_g, a_s, b_s)

 = beta(g[j] | a_g, b_g) * beta(s[j] | a_s, b_s) T[0, g[j]]

where the second truncation means to divide by the cdf of beta
up to g[j] with parameters a_s and b_s.

- Bob

>
> g[j]~beta(a_g,b_g) and s[j]~beta(a_s,b_s), with j=1,2,..,J.
>
>
>
>
> Em sábado, 30 de abril de 2016 18:22:02 UTC-3, Bob Carpenter escreveu:
> Your constraint is convenient because you're really
> asking for the first two components of the cumulative
> distribution over the simplex.
>
> data {
>   int<lower=0> J;
> }
> parameters {
>   simplex[3] theta[J];
> }
> transformed parameters {
>   vector[J] g;
>   vector[J] s;
>
>   g <- to_vector(theta[, 1]);
>   s <- g + to_vector(theta[, 2]);
> }
>
> Because beta(1, 1) is uniform, those priors on s and j won't
> do anything --- Stan only needs the log density up to a constant.
> So you can just drop them.
>
> The resulting prior is uniform over the (g,s) pairs meeting
> the constraint (the points in (0, 1) x (0, 1) above the diagonal).
>
> - Bob

[retitled]

The problem's that it can't evaluate the density for the first
iteration without error.  It's specifically telling you (by reporting
line number) that this line is going wrong:

    y_res    <- integrate_ode(ode1, y_ini, tsm[1, N_t_dose]- 0.0000001, tsm[2], ke, x_r, x_i);

and specifically ahs too large an initial time.  So you want to check
that tsm[1, N_t_dose] - 0.0000001 is correct in your inputs.

I retitled so that someone more familiar with the ODE errors than
me would see this and mayve have an idea what's going on.  It is
possible CmdStan and RStan vary in their ODE solver at this point
because it's been under construction.

- Bob

P.S.  Does your ODE have an analytic solution?  If so, that'd
      be a lot faster to fit.

messages.subject: Wiener diffusion model RT predictions
messages.subject_clean: Wiener diffusion model RT predictions
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm looking to generate response time predictions from a Wiener model in Stan. I'd like to prepare a plot to illustrate how well the model fits the RT data, and could use some advice on how best to go about this. Each trial has slightly different drift parameters, since the drift parameters are functions of trial-specific data. Here's my initial thought:

1) take the mean of the posterior for each parameter, and use this to calculate the drift parameters for each trial;
2) generate an RT distribution from these parameters, and take the mean of this distribution;
3) use this mean as the predicted RT for that trial.

Does this approach seem appropriate? Is there a clever way to achieve this with a couple lines in the generated quantities block? I obviously wouldn't estimate the model fit this way, but would like a fair way to illustrate it. Any advice much appreciated!

Best,
Tor

See the section on “Posterior Predictive Checks” in Bayesian Data Analysis.
You don’t want to compare means but rather entire predictive distributions of
return times to the measured return times.

Thank you for your attention, Bob Carpenter. I write the model code I am studying in Stan code, but the code did not work. Can you help me? I am working with a model called DINA and I'm having problems to implement it in Stan.

Below, write an abstract of this model:

A questionnaire with J questions is answered by $n$ individuals in order to classify each individual based upon mastery and nonmastery of the $K$ skills. We have 2^K possible attribute profiles. Example: For K=4: we have 2^4=16 differents profiles: alpha_1 = (0,0,0,0), alpha_2 = (1,0,0,0), alpha_3 = (0,1,0,0), ... , alpha_16 = (1,1,1,1). In case, alpha_2 is a profile that have skill 1 and don't have skill 2,3 and 4.

The skills needed to succeed on item j are stored in vector q_j=(q_j1,q_j2,...,q_jK), where q_jk is 1 if item j requires skill k and zero otherwise.

The random variable Y_ij|\alpha_i,\Omega_j ~ Bernoulli(P_ij) is one if the individual i answered correctly the item j and zero otherwise.
Omega_j = (s_j, g_j), where s_j and g_j are item parameters and P_ij = P(Y_ij=1|alpha_i,Omega_j) = ((1-s_j)^eta_ij)*(g_j^(1-eta_ij)) and
eta_ij = (alpha_i1^q_ij) * (alpha_i2^q_ij) * (alpha_i3^q_ij) * ... * (alpha_iK^q_ij)

I have the feeling that what I did in Stan's wrong. Follows the code attached.
For large volumes of data, the runtime is very large (48 hours to run in 1000 iterations).

2.  You can run into trouble when you put unnatural hard bounds on a parameter.  Here you have bounded sigma to be between .9 and maxPoly + 1.1.  This could create trouble. Similarly for your parameter that is bounded between 1 and 100 (although that’s commented out so it won’t affect your model as written here).

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

yes everything can be randomly initialized initialize except one parameter.

This parameter is "perturbation". since in my model I have to do

real_value_simplex = (observed_value .* perturbation)

I have to give to perturbation

1) prior with mode =1, ~ gamma(k, k-1), which is no problem

AND

2) an initial value of 1 to avoid parity problems, since perturbation can be multiplied .* 2 and still give the same real_value_simplex.

Is there a possibility to define init for only one parameter?

Stefano Mangiola

Data analyst @
Melbourne University
Hovens lab - Papenfuss lab
Royal Melbourne Hospital - WEHI
+61 (0)450135954

messages.subject: Impending R 3.3.0
messages.subject_clean: Impending R 3.3.0
messages.body_plain:
R version 3.3.0 is scheduled to be released May 3 sometime during the Western European day. If you use Stan regularly or need to use Stan this week, I would recommend not immediately updating R. That said, we are not anticipating any problems on a Mac (with a recent operating system) or Linux (unless you use Debian Unstable in which case you may need the next release of Rcpp to install rstanarm).

The biggest impact of R 3.3.0 will be on Windows because they have updated Rtools33 to use version 4.9-3 of the mingw compilers, after having used a prerelease of 4.6-3 for many, many years. Exceptions (which are a common occurrence when running Stan programs) are handled differently in the 4.9-3 version, so I think it is impossible to use Rtools32 with R 3.3.0 or to use Rtools33 with previous versions of R. Stan is workable with R 3.3.0 and Rtools33, but that does not mean that it will work for you on Windows. We probably have failed to anticipate some issues pertaining to bitness, CYGWIN, arbitrary corporate policies, Windows versions not equal to 7, etc., so to repeat: don't upgrade unless you know what you are doing. There are revised instructions on how to use Rtools33 on

https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Getting-Started

When upgrading, make sure that you do not (auto) load any stanfit or stanmodel objects that were created with a previous version of Rtools into your Global Environment on startup. This is a common source of problems when you select "yes" after it asks you if you want to save your workspace before quitting R. You can avoid this by always selecting "no" (which is what I do) or by deleting the .RData file (which may be hidden) from your default working directory.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: constrain shape parameters >0 in beta distribution
messages.body_plain:
You probably want that Pareto the other way around if it's to
match the manual.  That's the uniform on the log scale prior
that Andrew recommended in BDA.  He told me he doesn't like
that prior any more, but as far as I know, hasn't suggested
an alternative.  Probably because we almost always work on
the log-odds scale rather than directly with beta variates.

Also, if you have pi ~ pareto(epsilon, 1.5), then you
need to declare

  parameters<lower=epsilon> pi;

because that first parameter in the pareto is the lower bound.

- Bob

> On May 2, 2016, at 5:14 PM, Haoyan Sun <haoy...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks Ben!
> I set a Pareto prior for pi, as the manual suggested:  pi ~ pareto(1.5, 1); although it doesn't seem helping much.  Anyways, I am glad its not a big deal, thanks a lot!!
> Just out of curiosity, is it possible that for some transitions, inv_mu become 0 or 1 which causes a or b = 0 ?
>
> On Monday, May 2, 2016 at 1:46:07 PM UTC-7, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Monday, May 2, 2016 at 3:31:35 PM UTC-4, Haoyan Sun wrote:
> I didn't write out the parameter section in my question above, but I do declare pi as you suggested, otherwise I wouldn't even have sampling finished.
> So the sampling finishes ok, my problem is just the warning message that some shape parameter is 0. I don't know if I should just ignore the warning or there is a better way to reparametrize.
>
> If you have it parameterized like that, then the problem is simply that on some transitions pi underflowed to zero. In that case, it will reject the proposal but if it only happens a few times, it is not a big deal. You can perhaps avoid it by putting some prior on pi with vanishing density at zero.
>
> Ben
>
>

> R version 3.3.0 is scheduled to be released May 3 sometime during the Western European day. If you use Stan regularly or need to use Stan this week, I would recommend not immediately updating R. That said, we are not anticipating any problems on a Mac (with a recent operating system) or Linux (unless you use Debian Unstable in which case you may need the next release of Rcpp to install rstanarm).
>
> The biggest impact of R 3.3.0 will be on Windows because they have updated Rtools33 to use version 4.9-3 of the mingw compilers, after having used a prerelease of 4.6-3 for many, many years. See the end of the message.  To get rid of all these issues,
you can reduce step size and increase target acceptance rate.  The
problem is that floating point arithmetic can easily underflow and
overflow, espeically when there are exponentiation operations.  But
given this only happened once (that count of 1), it's no big deal,
as the error message tries to indicate.

Transformed parameters are always validated against their declared
constraints.

The message is problematic in that there's no Metropolis rejection
in NUTS (though there is in basic static HMC) --- it's slice sampled.

- Bob

messages.subject: Improving speed for ecological model
messages.subject_clean: Improving speed for ecological model
messages.body_plain:
I've been comparing the speed of Stan vs JAGS on some ecological models. In reading the book

Korner-Nievergelt et al (2015). Bayesian Data Analysis in Ecology Using Linear Models with R, BUGS, and Stan. (link to website with code) <http://www.oikostat.ch/blmeco.htm>

I ran across example 14.5 <http://www.oikostat.ch/blmeco/ch14/CJS_swallows.stan>, which is a mark-recapture model that uses a "trick" to avoid discrete latent parameters by integrating them out with a while loop (the parameter chi, which represents the probability of never seeing the animal again). The authors found it was substantially more efficient than WinBUGS. However, when I coded it myself in JAGS I incorporated this trick instead of modeling the discrete states directly, making the parameterization identical. And to my surprise JAGS was more efficient (minESS/time), albeit not that much. To me this suggests that it was removing the need to track the states directly that was the major difference.

I was quite surprised by that, and wondering if there are any computational improvements that can be made to the Stan model.

I looked through the manual and thought maybe trying to use ragged arrays. The variable `last` represents the last time period the animal was seen, effectively determining the size of the loop over time for that animal. But it is not clear to me how to implement them, or even if that is something worth trying in this case. I also considered using the "ones trick" from BUGS so that the likelihood statements could be vectorized, but wasn't sure how to wrangle the code to accomplish this.

Does anyone have any thoughts? Or is this just not the type of model that Stan would be expected to outperform JAGS?

Sure, if you want to run it you can use the attached model files, and data saved as an RDS file. I should note that to make the two models match I had to alter the originally linked Stan model. The rjags version isn't up on CRAN but can be found here:  https://sourceforge.net/projects/mcmc-jags/files/rjags/4/ and installed manually.  I was really curious to see the differences on identical parameterizations, hence all the extra leg work. The Stan model runs about the same as the original.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Improving speed for ecological model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Improving speed for ecological model
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for doing the legwork and writing in.

How are you calculating n_eff?  Stan is much more conservative
than JAGS (uses cross-chain information and also longer-term correlations)
and there can be huge differences in estimated effective sample size.

How big is the data set?  You'll find that HMC has more
of an advantage with more dimensions.

Marginalizing out parameters almost always helps with efficiency.  Especially
discrete ones that are difficult to mix with Gibbs sampling.

The Stan code isn't very efficient as written.

    for(j in 1:4){
      b0[j]~normal(0, 10);
      b1[j]~normal(0, 10);
      }

Vectorize to

  b0 ~ normal(0, 10);

Same for the other distributions.

This

  sigmayearphi~uniform(0,3);

doesn't match its declaration, which should include the upper bound:

  real<lower=0, upper=3> sigmayearphi;

The model should define a finite log density for any parameter
meeting the constraints.  With only lower=0, sigmayearphi = 4 satisfies
the constraint, but produces a -infinity log density.

You can pull the first line above the loop:

 for (k in 1:last[i]) {
        if(k>1) increment_log_prob(log(phi[i, k-1]));

and just use

  increment_log_prob(log(phi[i, 1:(last[i] - 1)]));

Those were the things that jumped out at me, but there may be
more if you can find expressions that are repeated --- you don't
want to every apply log or inv_logit or any other expensive function
to the same argument twice.

- Bob

> On May 3, 2016, at 6:22 PM, Cole Monnahan <mon...@uw.edu> wrote:
>

> I've been comparing the speed of Stan vs JAGS on some ecological models. In reading the book
>
> Korner-Nievergelt et al (2015). Bayesian Data Analysis in Ecology Using Linear Models with R, BUGS, and Stan. (link to website with code)
>
> I ran across example 14.5, which is a mark-recapture model that uses a "trick" to avoid discrete latent parameters by integrating them out with a while loop (the parameter chi, which represents the probability of never seeing the animal again). The authors found it was substantially more efficient than WinBUGS. However, when I coded it myself in JAGS I incorporated this trick instead of modeling the discrete states directly, making the parameterization identical. And to my surprise JAGS was more efficient (minESS/time), albeit not that much. To me this suggests that it was removing the need to track the states directly that was the major difference.
>
> I was quite surprised by that, and wondering if there are any computational improvements that can be made to the Stan model.
>
> I looked through the manual and thought maybe trying to use ragged arrays. The variable `last` represents the last time period the animal was seen, effectively determining the size of the loop over time for that animal. But it is not clear to me how to implement them, or even if that is something worth trying in this case. I also considered using the "ones trick" from BUGS so that the likelihood statements could be vectorized, but wasn't sure how to wrangle the code to accomplish this.
>
> Does anyone have any thoughts? Or is this just not the type of model that Stan would be expected to outperform JAGS?
>

Hi Bob, thanks for the reply. Unfortunately I had forgotten how much I changed from the original model, and you'll find that I've vectorized where possible in the previous email which had model files, data, inits, and a script to setup the runs. Sorry for the confusion, please take a look at the attached.

I mentioned on here a few months ago that I was doing some testing of JAGS and Stan, initially out of curiosity and as a check on my understanding. But I think it would be an illustrative paper for for many ecologists: an intuitive illustration of HMC and some practical speed tests vs the status quo JAGS. If this forum is a good place to discuss parameterizations and such then I might post a few other models.
.
A few inline thoughts  below.

On Tue, May 3, 2016 at 7:35 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> Thanks for doing the legwork and writing in.
>
> How are you calculating n_eff?  Stan is much more conservative
> than JAGS (uses cross-chain information and also longer-term correlations)
> and there can be huge differences in estimated effective sample size.
>

I'm using rstan::monitor() for both Stan and JAGS output. I've done this for a bunch of models and compare it to CODA estimates, and indeed it can be very different and the new way is almost always lower ESS.

> How big is the data set?  You'll find that HMC has more
> of an advantage with more dimensions.
>
> Marginalizing out parameters almost always helps with efficiency.  Especially
> discrete ones that are difficult to mix with Gibbs sampling.
>

JAGS isn't using Gibbs sampling here. It's using slice sampling (base::RealSlicer for all 177 parameters). I find that most of the ecology models I test typically use slice sampling, which leads to unexpected things like JAGS taking longer per iteration but having a higher ESS than Stan (the exact opposite of what is expected!), in some cases. So far I've discovered that it's hard to predict which platform is more efficient.

> The Stan code isn't very efficient as written.
>
>     for(j in 1:4){
>       b0[j]~normal(0, 10);
>       b1[j]~normal(0, 10);
>       }
>
> Vectorize to
>
>   b0 ~ normal(0, 10);
> Same for the other distributions.

As above, my fault for linking to an outdated file. I've done this.

>
> This
>
>   sigmayearphi~uniform(0,3);
>
> doesn't match its declaration, which should include the upper bound:
>
>   real<lower=0, upper=3> sigmayearphi;
>
> The model should define a finite log density for any parameter
> meeting the constraints.  With only lower=0, sigmayearphi = 4 satisfies
> the constraint, but produces a -infinity log density.
>

Yes I dropped that. I saw the discussion on eliminating the uniform prior density a while back, so took it out.

> You can pull the first line above the loop:
>
>  for (k in 1:last[i]) {
>         if(k>1) increment_log_prob(log(phi[i, k-1]));
>
> and just use
>
>   increment_log_prob(log(phi[i, 1:(last[i] - 1)]));
>
> Those were the things that jumped out at me, but there may be
> more if you can find expressions that are repeated --- you don't
> want to every apply log or inv_logit or any other expensive function
> to the same argument twice.
>
> - Bob

>
>
>
>
> > On May 3, 2016, at 6:22 PM, Cole Monnahan <mon...@uw.edu> wrote:
> >
> > I've been comparing the speed of Stan vs JAGS on some ecological models. In reading the book
> >
> > Korner-Nievergelt et al (2015). Bayesian Data Analysis in Ecology Using Linear Models with R, BUGS, and Stan. (link to website with code)
> >
> > I ran across example 14.5, which is a mark-recapture model that uses a "trick" to avoid discrete latent parameters by integrating them out with a while loop (the parameter chi, which represents the probability of never seeing the animal again). The authors found it was substantially more efficient than WinBUGS. However, when I coded it myself in JAGS I incorporated this trick instead of modeling the discrete states directly, making the parameterization identical. And to my surprise JAGS was more efficient (minESS/time), albeit not that much. To me this suggests that it was removing the need to track the states directly that was the major difference.
> >
> > I was quite surprised by that, and wondering if there are any computational improvements that can be made to the Stan model.
> >
> > I looked through the manual and thought maybe trying to use ragged arrays. The variable `last` represents the last time period the animal was seen, effectively determining the size of the loop over time for that animal. But it is not clear to me how to implement them, or even if that is something worth trying in this case. I also considered using the "ones trick" from BUGS so that the likelihood statements could be vectorized, but wasn't sure how to wrangle the code to accomplish this.
> >
> > Does anyone have any thoughts? Or is this just not the type of model that Stan would be expected to outperform JAGS?

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] testing how running time scales with iteration
messages.body_plain:
You want to run warmup until the adaptation has converged.
Anything less than 100 warmup iterations (200 total iterations
if you go with the default) is unlikely to do that, because
we're estimating variance components.  Note that converging
the adaptation isn't quite the same as getting to the
high-mass volume of the posterior;  you need to get to the
high mass part of the posterior, then spend some time there
in order to get the adaptation right.

After that, time per time per iteration and effective sample
size per iteration should be nearly linear.

This is all in CmdStan --- I don't know what the I/O and
memory allocation overhead is in PyStan or RStan;  they keep
the draws in memory, unlike CmdStan, which streams them to
a file.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Bob: attached are the files that should get you going. Also note that this requires JAGS 4.2.0 and rjags 4.4. The rjags version isn't up on CRAN but can be found here:  https://sourceforge.net/projects/mcmc-jags/files/rjags/4/ and installed manually. I've just been using the defaults in Stan for now:

adapt_delta=.8
max_treedepth=10
metric='diag_e'
warmup=N/2
and adaptation of stepsize turned on.

I've run them with Niter=200,000. Here's a little table of results.

model Npar max.cor JAGS Stan Stan/JAGS
swallows_nc 177 0.800 0.421 0.098 0.230
swallows 177 0.889 0.570 0.063 0.110

where the top row is with non-centered random effects and the bottom row centered. 'max.cor' is just the maximum correlation from draws of an independent sampler. The JAGS and Stan columns are minESS/time, and the last is the ratio. Stan is about 5-10 times slower. This is averaged over 10 random seeds and initial values. I've stored summary outputs about adaptation if that helps.

In some earlier tests I experimented with setting adapt_delta across a gradient (.5 to .99) and found no major improvement in efficiency, but admittedly that was with fewer iterations.

Thanks,
Cole

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublis

On May 4, 2016, at 6:22 PM, Cole Monnahan <mon...@uw.edu> wrote:

> Bob: attached are the files that should get you going. Also note that this requires JAGS 4.2.0 and rjags 4.4. The rjags version isn't up on CRAN but can be found here:  https://sourceforge.net/projects/mcmc-jags/files/rjags/4/ and installed manually. I've just been using the defaults in Stan for now:
>
> adapt_delta=.8
> max_treedepth=10
> metric='diag_e'
> warmup=N/2
> and adaptation of stepsize turned on.
>
> I've run them with Niter=200,000. Here's a little table of results.
>
> modelNparmax.corJAGSStanStan/JAGS
> swallows_nc1770.8000.4210.0980.230
> swallows1770.8890.5700.0630.110
>
> where the top row is with non-centered random effects and the bottom row centered. 'max.cor' is just the maximum correlation from draws of an independent sampler. The JAGS and Stan columns are minESS/time, and the last is the ratio. Stan is about 5-10 times slower. This is averaged over 10 random seeds and initial values. I've stored summary outputs about adaptation if that helps.
>
> In some earlier tests I experimented with setting adapt_delta across a gradient (.5 to .99) and found no major improvement in efficiency, but admittedly that was with fewer iterations.
>
> Thanks,
> Cole

Michael: yes I did this by running them both with a high thinning rate, checking Rhat and ESS, and then plotting marginal QQ plots. Attached are those two plots, the second is a multipage PDF with groups of parameters.

It was enough to convince me that the two posteriors were the same, and that sub-sampling 10 samples from them would be effectively independent, for use in rerunning with default with those as initial values . Assuming convergence, of course.

I've setup some R code that does all this work, given two model files, data, and whatever inputs for Stan you want (metric, adapt_delta, etc.). My idea is to plug some representative ecological models in to see how they do.

That would be pushing Stan to the limit even if the model were
more cleanly identified.  As is, this linear predictor

>  y[obs_in_day] ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha
>         +beta[s]*female[obs_in_day]
>       +to_vector(a_age[s,age[obs_in_day]])
>       +to_vector(a_edu[s,edu[obs_in_day]])
>       +to_vector(a_party_id[s,party_id[obs_in_day]])
>       +to_vector(a_race[s,race[obs_in_day]])
>       +gamma*vote_prev_dma[obs_in_day]
>       +to_vector(a_dma[s,dma[obs_in_day]]));
>   }}

is only weakly identified because of all the varying
intercepts.

Have you thought about only including intercepts for some
of the alternatives?  That is, if there are 5 age cohorts,
only include predictors for four of them and roll the last
into the intercept --- it can help with identification.  But
even with this kind of recoding, this scale of data's probably
more than Stan can handle.

Otherwise, I don't see any alternative other than subsampling
the data to fit, fitting pieces of the model separately, or
moving to an approximate algorithm like ADVI (which we don't
understand well in terms of how fits relate to the full Bayesian
posterior).

- Bob

> > > Bob: attached are the files that should get you going. Also note that this requires JAGS 4.2.0 and rjags 4.4. The rjags version isn't up on CRAN but can be found here:  https://sourceforge.net/projects/mcmc-jags/files/rjags/4/ and installed manually. I've just been using the defaults in Stan for now:

messages.body_plain:
I have to say THANKS for you suggestions Bob and all the community!

After your suggestion:

in b = simplex(a * x)         x ~ gamma(p, p-1) is not uniquely defined

I had few hard days to try 3 different alternatives to stabilize the model, than the simple and obvious solution came to me, and I want to share.

For making x with unique solution

we can do x ~ dirichlet([p_hat,p_hat,...p_hat])    in this case b = simplex(a * simplex()) works well.

I known probably is not the best explanation, but I'm open for any question :)

>

>
> - I added upper=100 because if there is no perturbation (perturbation = [1,1,....,1]), then bias_magnitude tends to Inf. I can leave withOUT upper, but then I should put a prior on bias_magnitude. What do you think?

> >   real<lower=1, upper=100> bias_magnitude;
> >   for(b in 1:num_batches) perturbation[b] ~ gamma(bias_magnitude, bias_magnitude-1);
> >
> > For efficiency, you can vectorize the loop as
> >
> >   perturbation ~ gamma(bias, bias - 1);
> >
>
> - Thanks. Also please not that perturbation is a matrix-like object
>
> > But when you do this:
> >
> >   for(k in 1:K) phi_hat_no_bias[k] <- phi_given[k] .* perturbation;

messages.subject: ODE solver
messages.subject_clean: ODE solver
messages.body_plain:
Hi Linas!

Whow, what a huge model! There are a couple of things you should (probably have to) consider:

- To my knowledge rstan supports an include functionality and for cmdstan you can find on this list a trick I published to make includes work as well

- Instead of includes I would recommend you to use the expose_stan_function in R. So you need to add a function, calculate_pred, or so which calculates y_hat for your model. Then you can export that to R and just call the function

- The most important one: Do not pass this huge vector into the ODE as parameters, but instead only pass the 1 parameter which you really want to estimate as parameter into the ODE RHS function!! All parameters which are constant should be passed into the function via x_r, the real array intended for data.

This last thing has to do with the fact that Stan is calculating internally gradients of the ODE solution with respect to the parameters. The ODE RHS function assumes that everything what you pass into it as 3. argument to be a parameter for which sensitivities are calculated. Getting those sensitivities is insanely numerically expensive and you should always try to keep the size of the array in the 3. argument position as small as possible and instead use the x_r for anything which does not change. You could, for example, use the x_i as int array to indicate which index in the parameter vector is varying, just an idea.

Note that Stan´s capabilities wrt to ODEs are getting much improved in the upcoming versions.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Improving speed for ecological model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Improving speed for ecological model
messages.body_plain:
Great question, Daniel!

In general, thinning loses information (lower n_eff)
compared to not thinning.

The reason Daniel's asking here is that thin=500 will mask long
autocorrelation times.  Suppose we have N iterations.
If one sampler has N / n_eff = 10 and the other has N / n_eff=100,
then thin = 500 is going to penalize the former sampler's
efficiency by a factor of 10.

So I'd be curious as to what the comparison looks like
for N=500, N=1000, and N=2000 without thinning.  What we've
found in almost every model we've carefully compared is
that Stan's faster when measured on a time per n_eff basis.

- Bob

> On May 5, 2016, at 10:17 AM, Cole Monnahan <mon...@uw.edu> wrote:
>
> Daniel: Sorry I meant for the table I sent previously. I don't have the unthinned long chains since thinning was done by the functions... stan(..,. thin=500) etc. When I do the actual ESS comparisons I don't do any thinning, since each Stan draw contains more information. -Cole
>

> Daniel: I forgot to mention earlier, there's no thinning for either JAGS or Stan in what I'm doing.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob (and Daniel), let me clarify a bit. I am only doing a thinning rate of 500 to verify that the JAGS and Stan models have the same posterior (Michael asked if I had done this, so I posted those plots). In this case I don't care at all about comparing efficiencies -- I'm simply trying to make sure it's valid to proceed with that stage of testing. Think of it as a debugging step.

All of my efficiency comparisons don't use thinning at all: all parameters are saved. Your example is exactly why I don't thin: it will penalize the more efficient sampler.

I have tried doing this with fewer iterations, and then (following advice I saw somewhere on here) doubled the iterations until at least it appears that Stan is adapting nicely. If anything this is unfair to JAGS because it wouldn't need as long of a warmup, but to keep things simple I use the same iterations and warmup (N/2) periods for both platforms.

I realize that it is difficult to do such comparisons fairly, as there are many moving pieces. I hope what I'm currently doing is fairly representative of what an end user would experience, particularly a new one migrating over from a BUGS variant.

Has anyone thought about trying to vectorize the likelihood calculations using a ragged array? That seemed to be the most obvious place to look for this model...

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Help: Is my ODE model misspecified, ill-constrained, or is something else wrong?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Help: Is my ODE model misspecified, ill-constrained, or is something else wrong?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the update.  This has been an ongoing issue for us
with parameters drifting into stiff regions and the simple Runge-Kutta
integrator "locking up" (basically reducing step size until it appears
to just hang).

The good news is that new stiff ODE solver we'll be rolling out in 2.10
should be much more robust.  And we've built in limits on the RK integrator.
(And when I say "we", this has mostly been done by Sebastian Weber based
on code originally written by Michael Betancourt.)

- Bob

> On May 5, 2016, at 9:00 AM, Elizaveta Semenova <elizaveta....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> As a note: my issue above was resolved through
>
> - feeding only unknown parameters (subject to inference) into the ODE as theta and other ODE-parameters (but not the parameters of the hierarchical model ) into the system as data x_r, x_i
>
> - changing the step size in the R call through
>
>   fit <- stan(..., control=list(stepsize=0.001, adapt_delta=0.9))
>
> Regards,
> Liza
>
>
> On Wednesday, May 4, 2016 at 3:41:01 PM UTC+2, Elizaveta Semenova wrote:
> Hello all,
>
> I am also working on a SIR model and have a similar issue: eternal fitting time. It does not occur for the one-parameter inference, but a real piece of work will involve much higher number of parameters and latent states.
> Even I read the discussion above, I am not sure whether I understand what the remedy is. Maybe someone could direct me.
>
> The attached R-file includes the following three steps:
> - generate SIR-data with noise (all parameters are known), extract values of y2 (Infected) to use it as input data for the inference,
> - run STAN with one parameter: this works fine,
> - same model with two parameters: runs forever.
>
> P.S. you may criticize the way I am creating and fitting noise since these are not two completely consistent procedures: in the fitting part I am not taking into account the cutoff that I am using to generate the noisy values. But I think (and the one-parameter inference supports the statement) it should not be a problem.
>
> Would be grateful for any help and critique,
> Liza.

> The NaN isn’t just dividing by zero — it can happen for various reasons
> depending on the floating point implementation.
>
> Having an R to S component could add enough feedback to make the
> ODEs stiff, but it’s hard to say until you share an updated model that
> properly uses measured states.  In particular, if you haven’t measured
> any S, I, or R states then there will be nothing to constrain your parameters
> and it wouldn’t be surprising if that non identified posterior stretched into
> pathological parameters.
>
> Additionally, even with a well-defined model it can be helpful to play
> with your initial conditions (say with init=0 or some small value) and
> start with a small step size to avoid poor adaptation.
>

>> Hi Michael,
>>
>> Your model is very helpful, and you shared it with me before; the model this one is abstracted from is based on it. Also, your point about the use of the ODE output on the LHS is correct, and I was not thinking clearly when incorporating that into my simplified model. (Altering it doesn't change the behavior)
>>
>> Perhaps the stiffness may be because this model has a feedback from the R compartment to the S compartment, unlike your model, but that can be a critical feature of the model - especially if modeling multiple seasons. Also, based on a quick check, eliminating it doesn't seem to help get it to converge it a reasonable amount of time, though there are no error messages now.
>>
>> I'm still unclear about why a stiff region of the ODE is leading to divide by 0 issues in sampling, but if that's not my problem, I guess I'll need to figure out what to do about the fact that there are stiff regions of the ODE - Do you have any ideas?
>>
>> Thanks,
>> David
>>
>> On Tuesday, November 10, 2015 at 1:40:46 PM UTC-8, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> That’s usually a sign that you’ve reached a stiff region of the system of ODEs,
>> but I’ve had no problem fitting SIR models in the past.  Your model seems to
>> be oddly constructed however, as there are no measured states.  In particular,
>> the output of the ODE should not on the LHS of any probability statement —

Interesting, we should try to understand this one.
A

> On May 5, 2016, at 12:03 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks for the clarification.  That's exactly how we've
> been doing evaluations ourselves. I appreciate the amount
> of effort you're putting in to do this right.
>
> I'm surprised that JAGS converges in fewer iterations
> than Stan does.  Is the newer version very different from
> older versions?
>
> - Bob
>
>> On May 5, 2016, at 11:59 AM, Cole Monnahan <mon...@uw.edu> wrote:
>>
>> Hi Bob (and Daniel), let me clarify a bit. I am only doing a thinning rate of 500 to verify that the JAGS and Stan models have the same posterior (Michael asked if I had done this, so I posted those plots). In this case I don't care at all about comparing efficiencies -- I'm simply trying to make sure it's valid to proceed with that stage of testing. Think of it as a debugging step.
>>
>> All of my efficiency comparisons don't use thinning at all: all parameters are saved. Your example is exactly why I don't thin: it will penalize the more efficient sampler.
>>
>> I have tried doing this with fewer iterations, and then (following advice I saw somewhere on here) doubled the iterations until at least it appears that Stan is adapting nicely. >>

>>

>>
>> In general, thinning loses information (lower n_eff)

>>

>> If one sampler has N / n_eff = 10 and the other has N / n_eff=100,

>> efficiency by a factor of 10.
>>

>> for N=500, N=1000, and N=2000 without thinning.  What we've
>> found in almost every model we've carefully compared is
>> that Stan's faster when measured on a time per n_eff basis.
>>
>> - Bob
>>

On Friday, May 6, 2016 at 12:19:52 AM UTC-4, Jessica Wong wrote:

In the non-symmetric case, you can't guarantee the eigenvalue is real and Stan doesn't do complex numbers.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Eigenvalue of non-symmetric matrix in Rstan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Eigenvalue of non-symmetric matrix in Rstan
messages.body_plain:
Can’t you just construct A^{T}A (or A^{T} A) directly, take the eigendecompositon
of that, and take the square-root of any positive eigenvectors directly?

The problem with anything else is that we need to compute gradients in Stan,
so we can’t just introduce arbitrary numerical algorithms that may not have
clean gradients.  If this eigenvalue will appear only as data, then you can
compute it externally and pass it into the Stan program.

messages.subject: Postdoctoral position in Alzheimer's epidemiology and clinical trials modelling
messages.subject_clean: Postdoctoral position in Alzheimer's epidemiology and clinical trials modelling
messages.body_plain:
Hello Stan users,

The Alzheimer's Disease Therapeutic Research Institute (http://atri.usc.edu/) is seeking postdoctoral scholars interested in modelling the long-term biomarker dynamics of Alzheimer's disease with the aim of informing clinical trial design. The project involves latent trait models for multidimensional longitudinal data, and preliminary work has been implemented in rstan.

We are an institute of the University of Southern California based in San Diego that coordinates clinical trials and natural history studies such as the Anti-Amyloid Treatment in Asymptomatic Alzheimer’s (A4) and Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) studies.

For more info, and to apply:

http://jobs.usc.edu/postings/65952
http://jobs.usc.edu/postings/65954

Many thanks,

Mike

--

Michael C Donohue, PhD
Associate Professor of Neurology
Associate Director of Biostatistics
Alzheimer’s Therapeutic Research Institute (ATRI <http://atri.usc.edu/>)
Keck School of Medicine of USC
University of Southern California

messages.subject: slightly off-topic : stan_trace plotting question
messages.subject_clean: slightly off-topic : stan_trace plotting question
messages.body_plain:
This isn't really a stan question, but it did
arise with one of the rstan plotting functions
and I haven't been able to solve it; so if there's
an easy solution, I'd very much like to know.

Suppose you're plotting the traces of a stanfit object
using stan_trace. You experiment a bit, and find
a layout that's pleasing, say nrow=6, ncol=2 per page.
You can now arrange a loop that plots params 1:12, then
13:24 etc.

The problem comes at the last page. Suppose you have
just two parameters left over. These two will fill
the entire page, and are quite out of scale with the
rest. Is there some easy way to avoid this? One
possibility might be to fill the rest of
the positions with empty plots (10, in my example)
but I don't know how to do this.

Thanks for any suggestions!

messages.body_plain:
This part of the error message is relevant to your error: "third argument to integrate_ode (initial times) must be data only and not reference parameters"

That's saying that the initial time, t0, must be declared and defined as data. It can't be a parameter.

I took a look at your Stan program and I couldn't really trace through the types of the variables, so I can't help out immediately. (I also think the last thing you sent doesn't work and I'm sure you had to fix some other things to make it work.)

I would really suggest simplifying and getting the simplest thing to work before building out something so complicated if you're still having trouble.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
hi charles,

thank you for your message.

would it be possible for you to share more details about your model? (if that's possible, of course.)

the fullrank version of advi is indeed experimental; we were able to successfully apply it to a small stochastic volatility model in our paper, but i'd love to learn more about how it's failing on your end. (http://www.proditus.com/papers/KucukelbirTran_2016.pdf)

cheers,
alp

messages.subject: random effects model in Stan
messages.subject_clean: random effects model in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Can somebody advice on the size of nonlinear mixed effects model that could be solved in Stan in reasonable time? For example items that are manufactured in batches exhibit intra-batch variability (items within same batch are different) while average for each batch is also different. This could be handled by two level hierarchical model and thus the number of parameters to estimate grow with increasing  # of batches. I wonder how many batches one may reasonably consider and are there any tricks to overcome dimensionality explosion problem. For instance, nonlinear mixed effects model might involve solution of ODEs.

Thank you,
Linas

messages.body_plain:
Stan is so impressive when it comes to many random effects, but the real bummer are ODEs! Just read the autodiff paper on arXiv on the scaling of the ODE system size and you quickly see how expensive ODEs are. On a different note, I just recently simplified an ODE Stan model from using ODEs to using an approximation to the ODE. I had 1400 subjects in the data set and the run time went down from 3 days to only ~4h (!) a factor of more than ~15x speedup (the model was still non-linear, just not using ODEs).

Long story short: Think twice if you can avoid the ODE... although we are working on improving these things, but for structural reasons, the price to pay for ODEs will be high regardless.

Sebastian

messages.subject_clean: Computing Hessian when the cost function consists of elementary functions
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

I am trying to use the stan C++ autodiff library for my visual pose tracking algorithm. Essentially I have a (reasonably complex) non linear cost function that warps a reference image and computes a difference measure between the warped and reference image. The parameters to my warp are defined by a 6 element vector (3 for translation, and 3 for rotation)

I have been able to get the Jacobian of my cost function using stan, but I'm stuck at trying to obtain the hessian. The crux of the problem comes down to elementary functions like sin and cos trying to operate on the stan::math::fvar<stan::math::var> template parameters. If I modify my code to explicitly use the .val() method to obtain the stan::math::var element, although the code compiles, I think the gradients aren't propagated, and so I get incorrect (0) jacobians and hessians.

Could someone please point me how to go about solving this issue? I tried to look at the sample code in earlier posts and unit test code, but they all use Eigen matrix elements, and not the simpler methods such as sin, cos, log. Is it the case that the master branch hasn't implemented the nested templatized math functions?

Thanks a lot!

Regards
Shaurya

messages.subject: speeding up k-fold cross validation
messages.subject_clean: speeding up k-fold cross validation
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I want to estimate predictive performance by k-fold cross validation (k=10) for a bunch of models. (I tried first  PSIS-LOO, but some of the models had  khats above 1) and I was wondering how to speed up  fitting 10 times each model.  I already know that these models converge with 2000 iteration with adapt_delta=.99,max_treedepth=12,stepsize=0.01, so I guess I can run only one chain with each partition. Is it right? (This way I could  run 10 models in parallel in 10 cores).
And my second question (which I hope is not completely stupid), can I reduce the warmup somehow by using information from the fitted models? and if so how/which information should I use?

Thanks!!
Bruno

I've been trying hierarchical multivariate auto / cross regressive time series, in both discrete and continuous time forms, using a Kalman filter to marginalise out latent states. Based on your comments I did a little more testing, and after further restricting the model / data I got fullrank to converge, though, in 15000 iterations rather than meanfield's 500. Regarding the eta estimation, it sometimes couldn't find an appropriate eta and sometimes suggested .1, so I just set it to that. I still seem to have some estimation inconsistency with full hmc for these models, probably the difficulties are related - it just seemed odd to me that meanfield would be so close to the final elbo straight away, and fullrank so far. If it still bugs me once I am more comfortable with the full model specification, I'll post again with the model / data. Just to know though, is it expected that fullrank would be orders of magnitude more difficult / slow? Based on current tentative results for these models I think NUTS is faster, though I'd also be interested in trying the stochastic sampling approach for large scale data at some point...

On Friday, May 6, 2016 at 9:53:50 PM UTC+2, Alp Kucukelbir wrote:
> hi charles,
>
> thank you for your message.
>
> would it be possible for you to share more details about your model? (if that's possible, of course.)
>
> the fullrank version of advi is indeed experimental; we were able to successfully apply it to a small stochastic volatility model in our paper, but i'd love to learn more about how it's failing on your end. (http://www.proditus.com/papers/KucukelbirTran_2016.pdf)
>
> regarding your concerns: i am not aware of any programming/implementation-level bug that specifically affects the fullrank version of advi. i reckon that the optimization for fullrank is more challenging than meanfield for your model and that the heuristic `eta` that we estimate is likely too large.
>
> cheers,
> alp

messages.subject_clean: error when variable declared in model block but not in parameters block
messages.body_plain:
On Sunday, May 8, 2016 at 2:55:23 AM UTC-4, Will Townes wrote:
> I'm a stan beginner trying to fit a hierarchical logistic regression (with random intercepts) using RStan. I was able to get the model to work when I put the vector of random intercepts into the parameters block. This results in a large output. I would prefer to exclude the intercepts from the output, which I understand can be done by declaring the variable inside the model block instead of in the parameters block. Yet, when I do that the sampler fails due to the following error:

That is a misunderstanding. You can exclude an intermediate quantity from the output by putting it in the model block or a local block within the transformed parameters block. But in this case the intercepts are primitive in which case they must be declared in the model block. The only way to exclude them from the output is by specifying

stan(filename, pars = "rand_ints", include = FALSE)

> [597] "Exception thrown at line 22: stan::math::normal_log: Random variable is nan, but must not be nan!"

This tells you that in line 22, the left hand side of the ~ is NaN, which is guaranteed by the structure of the second model because rand_ints is not defined before it is referenced.

Ben

messages.subject: one chain is not converging with the others
messages.subject_clean: one chain is not converging with the others
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan Experts,

I persistently run in the following problem, when I try to estimate more complex (possibly overparameterized) reinforcement learning models: one of the default 4 chains (2000 samples each, 1000 warmup) is/are consistenly “off” from the others usually malingering at the boudary of the parameter range. For example, when trying to estimate learning rates (range 0-1), one chain is sampling at or near zero, whereas the other 3 are in a normal (i.e. expected) range of around 0.6. The attached density and trace plot clearly exemplify the problem. Moreover, it is always a different chain that is “off” when I look at different parameters.

The question is: what can I do about it? Are there any specific settings to the HMC sampler that I can adjust to avoid 1 chain being stuck, even if that means I have to sample each chain longer?

Back in my JAGS/runjags days, I could examine the chains and then extend the sampling at the point where I left off. I could also drop one of the chains. This was convenient to a certain extent, but it did not help with the problem of different chains being “off” for different parameters. Is something like this even advisable, or am I breaking some of the fundamental rules of MCMC sampling?

I have coded some post-processing functions in R that try to guess if a posterior distribution is bimodal due to one chain being "off" and — based on this judgment — attempts to remove the outlyling chain by replacing the samples of NA. I recoded parts of the WAIC function to deal with NAs in the log_lik parameter. Interestingly, this always results in a slightly higher WAIC (about 5 points) than the original model. Furthermore, I also recompute posterior point estimates (mean,map,median) based on these adjusted chains, which I need for further analyses. I would like to know, if the experts think this is a practical, but also viable solution to deal with the problem or whether this is totally absurd.

Thanks a lot,
Jan

PS: attached are exemplary density and trace plots (these are actually the group posteriors, but I see this also with posteriors for individual subjects) and the stan model file that consistently produces this erratic behavior.

messages.subject: Model consultation for linear mixed effects: Stan mixing really poorly
messages.subject_clean: Model consultation for linear mixed effects: Stan mixing really poorly
messages.body_plain:
I'm wondering if someone can give me some advice for improving mixing for a model.

I'm trying to recreate an analysis from a paper that used the R package glmmMCMC to analyse a fairly complex linear mixed effects model. The model is from quantitative genetics and was analyzed as example 4 in this study: http://icesjms.oxfordjournals.org/content/early/2014/12/03/icesjms.fsu213.abstract

Here is the R formula version of the model:
body_weight ~ Reciprocal_Cross + degree_days_centered, random =
              ~animal + Dam + Tank_ID + ID

There are 1338 observations (rows). There are 15 fixed effects (Reciprocal_Cross and degree_days_centered) including 5 variance terms. The random effect sizes are: 1338 for animal, 183 for Dam, 57 for Tank_ID and 39 for ID. The whole point is the partition the variance.

I tried fitting this in Stan and JAGS, and found that JAGS was significantly faster for both the centered and non-centered ('.nc') versions of the model.

Here's a quick table from runs with 20,000 iterations and adapt_delta=0.9:

stan jags stan.nc <http://stan.nc> jags.nc <http://jags.nc>
time 1269.7 94.87 3140.25 154.34
minESS 12.3912 11.1872 24.2888 13.0488
minESS/time 0.0098 0.1179 0.0077 0.0845

The hypervariance controlling the animal random effects, which there is one for each observation, is the bottleneck here, although both Stan and JAGS seem to struggle with multiple parameters (see attached plot which shows ordered ESS for the 4 models).

I've been working through Michael's paper on hierarchical models for HMC (http://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.0906.pdf) and understand the implications for hypervariances with so much influence on the log posterior and the issues that arise from it. However, short of using RMHMC, I'm not sure how to "fix" it.

Presumably I could try to rewrite the likelihood statement to be in matrix notation, but that wouldn't affect the mixing only the time per transition. Is this type of model just really tough for HMC in it's current state? Is this a model we would expect JAGS to do better b/c it's a linear mixed effects model? (BTW JAGS is using slice sampling for variances and "glm::Albert-Chib" for everything else).

I've attached data, model files, and an R script to recreate the table and attached figure.

Thanks ahead of time,
Cole

Hi, you don’t want this real<lower=0,upper=10> stuff.  Instead just do real<lower=0> and put informative priors on these scale parameters, for example normal(0,1).  You are doing t_2(0,1) which could be ok—I don’t know enough about our example—but these long tails may not be needed.

SImilarly for a and b, don’t do normal(0,1e5), do something like normal(0,1) or normal(0,10).  In this case you should probably do normal(A,B) with weak priors on A and B.  No need to let the parameters completely float, that’s just asking for trouble.

Also no need for all those square roots, you can just parametrize scale paraemters directly.

Another thing is that you might want to center your linear predictor (“days”); if it is far from 0, this can give you big posterior correlations.

Also, have you tried simply fitting the model in rstanarm?  I’m curious how that would work for this example.

This is definitely the sort of example that we _don’t_ want Stan to have trouble with!

A

The real problem here is that neither Stan nor JAGS are able

When you have 10K iterations and n_eff values of 10,

messages.body_plain:
> The real problem here is that neither Stan nor JAGS are able
> to fit your model as specified.
>
> When you have 10K iterations and n_eff values of 10,
> it means something's not working.

We only ever have _estimates_ for the effective sample size,
and those estimators are notoriously finicky.  In particular, if
n_eff / n_transitions < 0.001 then there is no way that you have
enough information in your chains to construct a reasonable
n_eff estimate.

Immediately this invalidates your quantitative results, as you’re
comparing the small n_eff which is the most susceptible to bias
(let alone noise)  The n_eff plots demonstrate this clearly —
Stan is sampling far more parameters reasonably well than
JAGS, although even this should be interpreted carefully given
the interval of vanishing n_eff.  If _any_ of the parameters have
low n_eff then you have to consider that all of the other parameters
are sampling not from the joint distribution but rather the conditional
distribution with those low n_eff parameters essentially set to constants.

This is why comparisons to JAGS are so hard — the JAGS samplers
are really hard to diagnose and end up taking a huge amount of time
to verify.  Whereas when HMC hits problems it makes that clear immediately.
I won’t even get into how frustrating it is trying to recreate published
analyses that blindly trust fits out of packages like glmmMCMC...

As Andy notes, get rid of the sqrts and just model the deviations
directly.  Don’t use uniform priors and instead stick to soft
constraints.

As Bob notes, any strong nonlinearity in the model is a potential
cause of sampling problems.  Because there’s only one slope,
standardizing days (or body weight for that matter) won’t have
a huge effect.  There is however, an immediate problems
with your model.

There’s no global mean for all the ypred.  If <ypred> isn’t
zero then this forces the distribution of random effects to be
biased away from zero which causes tension with the priors
(which wants them to be distributed around zero) and induces
non-identifiabilities (as there are many ways the random effects
can trade off to achieve some non-zero bias).

Also, centering a will help speed up adaptation in Stan.

parameters {
  // fixed effects
  real b;

  // hyper variances
  real<lower=0> sigma_animal;
  real<lower=0> sigma_id;
  real<lower=0> sigma_tank;
  real<lower=0> sigma_dam;
  real<lower=0> sigma;

  // random effects
  real alpha;
  real alpha_cross_raw[n_cross];
  real alpha_animal_raw[n_animal];
  real alpha_id_raw[n_ID];
  real alpha_tank_raw[n_Tank_ID];
  real alpha_dam_raw[n_Dam];
}

model {
  real ypred[N];
  for(i in 1:N)
    ypred[i] <-   b * days[i] + alpha_cross_raw[cross[i]] * 100 + alpha
                + alpha_animal_raw[animal[i]] * sigma_animal;
                + alpha_id_raw[ID[i]] * sigma_id;
                + alpha_tank_raw[Tank_ID[i]] * sigma_tank;
                + alpha_dam_raw[Dam[i]] * sigma_dam;

  // Priors:
  b ~ normal(0, 100);

  alpha ~ normal(0, 10);
  alpha_cross ~ normal(0, 1);
  alpha_animal_raw ~ normal(0, 1)
  alpha_id_raw ~ normal(0, 1)
  alpha_tank_raw ~ normal(0, 1)
  alpha_dam_raw ~ normal(0, 1)

  sigma_animal ~ student_t(2,0,1);
  sigma_id ~ student_t(2,0,1);
  sigma_tank ~ student_t(2,0,1);
  sigma_dam ~ student_t(2,0,1);
  sigma ~ student_t(2,0,1);

  // likelihood
  body_weight~normal(ypred, sigma);

}

messages.body_plain:
hi charles,

it's hard to tell when meanfield vs. fullrank gives an easier
optimization problem. this is an open research question.

it could be that the meanfield problem has a local optimum that is
close to the initialization; that would explain the fast
"convergence".

in terms of speed: p = # of parameters in your model. meanfield is
o(p), fullrank is o(p^2).

cheers,
alp

messages.body_plain:
An advisor of Ghislain's here. Thought I'd sex-up his query by describing the context of his data/model:

We're looking at the performance of baseball umpires judging close plays at first base and examining whether different types of attention instructions affect this performance. We show each umpire videos of lots of plays, each play with a slightly different timing between the ball and runner's arrival at the base. For some blocks of plays we instruct the umpires to keep their attention on the base, and for other blocks we instruct the umpires to keep their attention on the baseman's glove.

For a given umpire and instruction condition we expect the probability of calling a play as "safe" (vs "out") as a binomial draw where the probability is a s-shaped function of the timing between the ball and runner reaching the base. So, high probability of saying "safe" on trials where the runner arrives well before the ball (large positive values of x) and low probability of saying "safe" on trials where the ball arrives well before the runner, and a smooth s-shaped transition between these two extremes.

We use the cumulative normal to achieve the s-shape because the mean-and-sd parameterization allows us to speak directly to bias (shift in the S, indexed by the cumulative normal's mean) and discrimination sensitivity (sharpness of the S, inversely indexed by the cumulative normal's sd). Since we have many umpires, we model this bias & sensitivity hierarchically, and implement an "intercept+-effect" coding to look at the effect of the attention instructions on both bias & sensitivity (again, both hierarchically). All the hierarchical sampling is done via a multivariate distribution, thus including inference on the potential for correlations amongst the parameters across the population of umpires.

When we run the model against real data, the posterior on the parameters associated with bias seem to be identical to the priors specified for those parameters regardless of said specification. So clearly we've erred somewhere, but we can't quite see where. Any ideas?

Mike

messages.body_plain:
The model's too complex for me to understand just by looking
at it, but I suspect this may be your problem:

  trial_pss[this_obs] <- pss_intercept_per_id[id[this_obs]]
                         + pss_effect_per_id[id[this_obs]] * condition[L] ;

Shouldn't that L be this_obs?  Otherwise, you get the same observation
for each condition and condition[1:(L - 1)] is otherwise unused.

I also didn't understand why you're doing this:

  real<lower=0,upper=pi()/2> zpopulation_pss_intercept_sd;

  population_pss_intercept_sd <- tan(zpopulation_pss_intercept_sd);

We generally recommend

  real<lower=0> zpopulation_pss_intercept_sd;

and then some kind of weakly informative prior such as

  zpopulation_pss_intercept_sd ~ normal(0, 2);

based on the expected scale of the variable for which this is
the scale parameter.

Our general advice is to start with simple models (e.g., no random
effects, fewer predictors, no covariance structure, etc.), fit them to
simulated data to make sure they work, then gradually build them up.
It's much easier to debug that way than starting with a complex
model.  As we say in computer science, design top down, code bottom up.
We need to make all this advice clear in the book we're writing!  The
manual just presents finished models without showing how we got there.

Also, this coding

  vector[4] beta[N];

  for (this_id in 1:N)
    beta[this_id] ~ multi_student_t(1,zeros,cor) ;

forces N solutions of the cor matrix.  It'll be much much
more efficient as

  matrix[N, 4] beta;

  to_vector(beta) ~ multi_student_t(1, zeros, cor);

Also, one degree of freedom in the T is giving you a very broad likelihood.
So when I meant start simple, remove the correlation structure, use normals,
etc.  Then when you add things, you'll know where they go wrong.

- Bob

P.S.  I would also strongly recommend against using tabs in computer
      programs --- they render differently depending on the context because
      there's no universal tab width.

P.P.S.  Though it doesn't matter for efficiency, it's easier to replace

for (i in 1:4) zeros[i] <- 0;

with

  zeros <- rep_vector(0, 4);

Thanks! This does just what I wanted. For those wanting a quick template, here's what I did, where mod is a stanfit object:

library(gridextra)

    p<-lapply(1:length(names(mod)), function(x) stan_trace(mod, pars=names(mod)[x]))

you may want to add   top=""  to the call to marrange: this omits the
"page m of n" headers. And if you are using a large-ish number of rows you might want to try

rstan_ggtheme_options(axis.title=element_text(size=10))

which reduces the font size of the parameter identifiers on the left.

messages.subject: Poor mixing of chains in model with randomly sampled errors - pointers?
messages.subject_clean: Poor mixing of chains in model with randomly sampled errors - pointers?
messages.body_plain:
I'm running models in STAN to try to estimate parameters in a bi-exponential function describing pathogen die-off:

ln(C(t)) = ln(C(0)) + ln(a*e^(-k1*t)+(1-a)*e^(-k2*t))

Where C(t) is a function of pathogen concentration over time t, C(0) is the initial concentration, a is a proportion of pathogens undergoing rapid decay specified by rate parameter k1, and 1-a is the complementary proportion undergoing slower die-off. In the model, a is estimated based on the location of the zero of the third derivative of the function, which is constrained by timepoints at which measurements were taken (can't be earlier than point midway between first two observations, can't be later than second to last data point).

Some experimental data for which I'm attempting to estimate parameters include measures of uncertainty and others don't. To attempt to integrate both data types into the same framework, I've created a model (attached) that imputes errors at each observed concentration timepoint according to a gamma distribution fit to the reported errors from other experiments at the same time as attempting to estimate the decay parameters. The model seems to run reasonably well much of the time, though chains will occasionally get stuck in particular regions of the sample space (see goodrun_trace.pdf, goodrun_dens.pdf, goodrun_data.pdf). Occasionally I run into a set of experimental data for which the effective sample size is very low, even for extremely high (>1,000,000) numbers of iterations (see badrun_trace.pdf, badrun_dens.pdf, badrun_data.pdf). In these cases, I've observed that the mixing of chains is quite poor, and chains spend more time stuck in narrow ranges of the probability space.

Are there any adjustments to model specification or data transformation that I should consider in order to eke out better performance? I have a relatively simplistic understanding of the workings of STAN at this point, so if there is material I should familiarize myself with prior to soliciting specific input, I would welcome direction towards that as well.

messages.body_plain:
It’s not so much a question of efficiency but rather exploration.
If the posterior had tails as heavy as the the tails of the Cauchy
distribution then HMC would struggle to explore the entirely of
that tail (although it would do far better than other samplers).
In this case the reparameterization would be useful as the
transformed space would feature much nicer tails.

But that would only be a factor here if your model were
non-informative, and even then HMC does okay when a
only a few parameters have heavy tails.

Ultimately this is an example of premature optimization.
As Bob notes, start simple and build up, adding these
reparameterization tricks only when necessitated by
poor performance.*

*Caveat: in hierarchical models it’s okay to default to
non-centered parameterizations given that most models
add hierarchical structure exactly because the data are
not super informative, which is where the non-centered
parameterization performs best.

On Saturday, May 7, 2016 at 10:04:09 AM UTC+3, Bruno Nicenboim wrote:
> Hi,
> I want to estimate predictive performance by k-fold cross validation (k=10) for a bunch of models. (I tried first  PSIS-LOO, but some of the models had  khats above 1) and I was wondering how to speed up  fitting 10 times each model.  I already know that these models converge with 2000 iteration with adapt_delta=.99,max_treedepth=12,stepsize=0.01, so I guess I can run only one chain with each partition.

Running several chains would be better. What is the n_eff for the quantity you are interested in now? What would be the expected n_eff with one chain? Would that be large enough for your purposes? Could you manage with several shorter chains?

> Is it right? (This way I could  run 10 models in parallel in 10 cores).
> And my second question (which I hope is not completely stupid), can I reduce the warmup somehow by using information from the fitted models? and if so how/which information should I use?

Since we can assume that posteriors for each fold are close to the full posterior, it would be possible to initialise the mass matrix and other adapted parameters to save time on the adaptation phase, and you could intialise parameter values using the samples from the full posterior samples, but still you could save less than 50% time. And I think it's not yet possible to skip the adaptation yet.

So my suggestion is to run several shorter chains for each cv-fold. Shorter warm-up should be enough if you initialise the parameters for each run from the full posterior samples (different values for each chain)

Aki

messages.subject_clean: speeding up k-fold cross validation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bruno!

I just recently was in the same trouble to be force to refit a Stan model over and over again to almost the same data. What I figured would be to transform my parameters to unit scale and 0 centered. So from your runs you know the posterior sd and center. Parametrize your model such that everything lives on the unconstrained space. Then you can use something like this scheme:

parameter block:
vector[K_phi] phi_raw;

transformed block:
  // shift and scale such that raw parameters are 0 centered and have
  // scale 1
  phi <- location_phi + scale_phi .* phi_raw;

The location_phi and scale_phi are the posterior estimates from previous runs (take mean and sd or use robust alternatives). You can still place a prior on phi since the Jacobian is a constant here, but the variables being sample are at unit scale around 0. Since warmup is actually about finding these scales and the centers, you can then shortcut warmup dramatically. There are 3 phases during warmup (explained in the manual) - I simply shortened these to 1/4 and my warmups are now roughly 3x times as fast. I also run a sanity check in that at the end of the fit I check Rhat being below 1.2 for all stuff I care about. If this is not the case, then I rerun Stan with a longer warmup (only cut down by 1/2) and hope things are fine.

This procedure is really a big step forward for me, but it can be dangerous, of course, but should work well in your setting.

Ah, don't forget to initilize phi_raw with unit normals or better make it under-dispersed, so N(0, 1/4); albeit the correct way would be to use N(0, 2) to my understanding, but this will probably only cost you more computation time to get warmup going, so an sd of 1/4 is safer.

Sebastian

Thank you for your suggestion. I am trying to estimate the transmission parameter of the SIR model using Stan, then use that to estimate basic reproductive number, which is the maximum eigenvalue of the next generating matrix (A). So the eigenvalue does not appear as data.

I tried your suggestion but found out that eigenvalue of A^{T}A is not the same that of A when A is nonsymmetric. Here is my code:

A <- matrix(c(-149,-50,-154,537,180,546,-27,-9,-25), nrow=3, ncol=3, byrow=T)

A2 <- A%*%t(A)

eigen(A)$value # 3 2 1

sqrt(eigen(A2)$value) # 8.177597e+02 2.474974e+00 2.964524e-03

I have tried other reading in the past few days but still couldn't come up with a better solution in order to get the eigenvalue of a asymmetric matrix in Stan. Please do you have other idea?

Regards

Jessica

> > > > I am trying to get the eigenvalue for a non-symmetric matrix. In R, we can use the eigen() function. However, I can only find a similar function in Rstan for only symmetric matrix call eigenvales_sym(). Any suggestions how I can get that eigenvalue in Rstan?

messages.body_plain:
There's nothing for approximate ODEs in there now.  If you want
to contribute C++ code for new functions, we have some Wiki pages
to help you follow the process.  But just coding a function in
Stan itself is going to be just as efficient as doing it in C++
unless you implement custom derivatives.

This is one of the goals of our new ONR grant, so we'll
be working on some approximate solutions ourselves.  I don't
know mucha bout it, so can't say anything more specific.

- Bob

Bob,

Currently ODEs are handled by something like:
y_hat <- integrate_ode(sho, y0, t0, ts, theta, x_r, x_i);

I thought that it should be possible to replace integrate_ode with some custom code [my_integrate_ode(y0, t0, ts, theta, x_r, x_i)] which calculates y_hat for each time point in ts. Current integrate_ode does exact integration. I am thinking about replacing it with approximate integration where system of ODEs is replaced by a system of algebraic equations. Recently I saw posts where folks are using splines to achieve the same purpose. Unfortunately it is impossible to code this in Stan modeling language, one has to do this in C++ (at least this is my understanding which may be wrong). What are the guidelines/requirements to create custom function my_integrate_ode?

Thank you,
Linas

messages.subject: discrepancy between sampled posteriors and underlying true parameters in a reinforced poisson proces
messages.subject_clean: discrepancy between sampled posteriors and underlying true parameters in a reinforced poisson proces
messages.body_plain:
Hello!
I am building a model of citation dynamics of the law based on http://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0778, which proposes a reinforced poisson process. To test my model, I generated data according to that stochastic process. My data thus consists of 1000 vectors of variable length, each representing the attentions received by a putative document. I fixed all the parameters except for the "intrinsic importance" parameter lambda. This parameter I drew from a Gamma(1.2,scale=0.8) distribution. I also randomly drew T, the end of the observation period, which is an observed quantity that enters the model. The model as well as my stan code are in the attachment.
I am having some difficulty interpreting the discrepancy between the lambda values I drew when I generated the data and the posterior samples I obtain. The attached png figure shows that in general the estimated lambdas don't have as large a spread and do not give a 1-1 linear relationship with my original lambdas. The original data include some high values for the lambdas but the draws from the posteriors of those high value lambdas are much smaller. The only draws showing high lambdas are for short vectors (usually associated with smaller lambdas since lambda influences how many citations a document will attract) because of the large uncertainty.
Since I eventually need to also estimate the other parameters and the hyper-parameters (the parameters of the gamma), I am quite worried to see that even this first step gives me unreliable inferences. I would appreciate any ideas regarding where things might be going wrong. I am happy to provide the code by which I generated the data in the first place.
Thank you for your help!
Marion

messages.body_plain:
How many dimensions do you have?  At the very least,
it's going to require N^2 * 20 bytes plus about 40
bytes per operator/function call in computing the function
and its gradient.

The reason to use autodiff is that finite differences
have low precision and you need to nest one inside the other
to calculate Hessians.  We only use the finite diffs to
validate our higher-order autodiff code---we don't recommend
using them for real work.

The hessian() code does call recover_memory() after each row
is computed.  We should probably modify it to define H(i,j) = H(j,i)
just to make sure everything's symmetric.

- Bob

On Monday, May 9, 2016 at 12:39:35 AM UTC-7, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>
> > The real problem here is that neither Stan nor JAGS are able
> > to fit your model as specified.
> >
> > When you have 10K iterations and n_eff values of 10,
> > it means something's not working.
>
> We only ever have _estimates_ for the effective sample size,
> and those estimators are notoriously finicky.  In particular, if
> n_eff / n_transitions < 0.001 then there is no way that you have
> enough information in your chains to construct a reasonable
> n_eff estimate.
>
> Immediately this invalidates your quantitative results, as you’re
> comparing the small n_eff which is the most susceptible to bias
> (let alone noise)  The n_eff plots demonstrate this clearly —
> Stan is sampling far more parameters reasonably well than
> JAGS, although even this should be interpreted carefully given
> the interval of vanishing n_eff.  If _any_ of the parameters have
> low n_eff then you have to consider that all of the other parameters
> are sampling not from the joint distribution but rather the conditional
> distribution with those low n_eff parameters essentially set to constants.
>
> This is why comparisons to JAGS are so hard — the JAGS samplers
> are really hard to diagnose and end up taking a huge amount of time
> to verify.  Whereas when HMC hits problems it makes that clear immediately.
> I won’t even get into how frustrating it is trying to recreate published
> analyses that blindly trust fits out of packages like glmmMCMC...
>
> As Andy notes, get rid of the sqrts and just model the deviations
> directly.  Don’t use uniform priors and instead stick to soft
> constraints.
>
> As Bob notes, any strong nonlinearity in the model is a potential
> cause of sampling problems.  Because there’s only one slope,
> standardizing days (or body weight for that matter) won’t have
> a huge effect.  There is however, an immediate problems
> with your model.
>
> There’s no global mean for all the ypred.  If <ypred> isn’t
> zero then this forces the distribution of random effects to be
> biased away from zero which causes tension with the priors
> (which wants them to be distributed around zero) and induces
> non-identifiabilities (as there are many ways the random effects
> can trade off to achieve some non-zero bias).
>
> Also, centering a will help speed up adaptation in Stan.
>
> parameters {
>   // fixed effects
>   real b;
>
>   // hyper variances
>   real<lower=0> sigma_animal;
>   real<lower=0> sigma_id;
>   real<lower=0> sigma_tank;
>   real<lower=0> sigma_dam;
>   real<lower=0> sigma;
>
>   // random effects
>   real alpha;
>   real alpha_cross_raw[n_cross];
>   real alpha_animal_raw[n_animal];
>   real alpha_id_raw[n_ID];
>   real alpha_tank_raw[n_Tank_ID];
>   real alpha_dam_raw[n_Dam];
> }
>
> model {
>   real ypred[N];
>   for(i in 1:N)
>     ypred[i] <-   b * days[i] + alpha_cross_raw[cross[i]] * 100 + alpha
>                 + alpha_animal_raw[animal[i]] * sigma_animal;
>                 + alpha_id_raw[ID[i]] * sigma_id;
>                 + alpha_tank_raw[Tank_ID[i]] * sigma_tank;
>                 + alpha_dam_raw[Dam[i]] * sigma_dam;
>
>   // Priors:
>   b ~ normal(0, 100);
>
>   alpha ~ normal(0, 10);
>   alpha_cross ~ normal(0, 1);
>   alpha_animal_raw ~ normal(0, 1)
>   alpha_id_raw ~ normal(0, 1)
>   alpha_tank_raw ~ normal(0, 1)
>   alpha_dam_raw ~ normal(0, 1)
>
>   sigma_animal ~ student_t(2,0,1);
>   sigma_id ~ student_t(2,0,1);
>   sigma_tank ~ student_t(2,0,1);
>   sigma_dam ~ student_t(2,0,1);
>   sigma ~ student_t(2,0,1);
>
>   // likelihood
>   body_weight~normal(ypred, sigma);
>
> }
>
>
