messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

To follow up, setting open_progress = FALSE worked (i.e., printed progress to the console). However, I subsequently encountered another, possibly related problem involving the parallel package. After running Stan for several days (a short run doesn’t yield this problem), I encounter the following fatal error after all Stan chains have finished:
> Error in checkForRemoteErrors(val) :
>   4 nodes produced errors; first error: cannot open the connection
> Warning message:
> In file(file, "r") :
>   cannot open file '/var/folders/67/k5k525tx2r39f09_y5zj7cbw0000gn/T//Rtmpck6AID/file9e1424c1bc2': No such file or directory

For the record, checkForRemoteErrors is from the parallel package and is defined thusly:
> function (val) {
>     count <- 0
>     firstmsg <- NULL
>     for (v in val) {
>         if (inherits(v, "try-error")) {
>             count <- count + 1
>             if (count == 1)
>                 firstmsg <- v
>         }
>     }
>     if (count == 1)
>         stop("one node produced an error: ", firstmsg, domain = NA)
>     else if (count > 1)
>         stop(count, " nodes produced errors; first error: ",
>             firstmsg, domain = NA)
>     val
> }

I suspect that what is happening here is that parallel (like rstan when open_progress = TRUE) creates a temporary file in the var directory that is being deleted sometime during the Stan run. So when checkForRemoteErrors looks for the file after Stan is finished, it can’t find it. Perhaps some program of mine is periodically “cleaning up” the var folder. If anyone has an ideas about what is going on, I would love to hear it. I am running a Mac Pro (Late 2013) with El Capitan.

Devin

>
> Bruno
>
>
> On Tue, May 10, 2016 at 10:35 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Bruno!
>
> I just recently was in the same trouble to be force to refit a Stan model over and over again to almost the same data. What I figured would be to transform my parameters to unit scale and 0 centered. So from your runs you know the posterior sd and center. Parametrize your model such that everything lives on the unconstrained space. Then you can use something like this scheme:
>
> parameter block:
> vector[K_phi] phi_raw;
>
> transformed block:
>   // shift and scale such that raw parameters are 0 centered and have
>   // scale 1
>   phi <- location_phi + scale_phi .* phi_raw;
>
>
> The location_phi and scale_phi are the posterior estimates from previous runs (take mean and sd or use robust alternatives). You can still place a prior on phi since the Jacobian is a constant here, but the variables being sample are at unit scale around 0. Since warmup is actually about finding these scales and the centers, you can then shortcut warmup dramatically. There are 3 phases during warmup (explained in the manual) - I simply shortened these to 1/4 and my warmups are now roughly 3x times as fast. I also run a sanity check in that at the end of the fit I check Rhat being below 1.2 for all stuff I care about. If this is not the case, then I rerun Stan with a longer warmup (only cut down by 1/2) and hope things are fine.
>
> This procedure is really a big step forward for me, but it can be dangerous, of course, but should work well in your setting.
>
> Ah, don't forget to initilize phi_raw with unit normals or better make it under-dispersed, so N(0, 1/4); albeit the correct way would be to use N(0, 2) to my understanding, but this will probably only cost you more computation time to get warmup going, so an sd of 1/4 is safer.
>
> Sebastian
>
> On Tuesday, May 10, 2016 at 10:09:24 AM UTC+2, Aki Vehtari wrote:
>
>
> On Saturday, May 7, 2016 at 10:04:09 AM UTC+3, Bruno Nicenboim wrote:
> Hi,
> I want to estimate predictive performance by k-fold cross validation (k=10) for a bunch of models. (I tried first  PSIS-LOO, but some of the models had  khats above 1) and I was wondering how to speed up  fitting 10 times each model.  I already know that these models converge with 2000 iteration with adapt_delta=.99,max_treedepth=12,stepsize=0.01, so I guess I can run only one chain with each partition.
>
> Running several chains would be better. What is the n_eff for the quantity you are interested in now? What would be the expected n_eff with one chain? Would that be large enough for your purposes? Could you manage with several shorter chains?
>
> Is it right? (This way I could  run 10 models in parallel in 10 cores).
> And my second question (which I hope is not completely stupid), can I reduce the warmup somehow by using information from the fitted models? and if so how/which information should I use?
>
> Since we can assume that posteriors for each fold are close to the full posterior, it would be possible to initialise the mass matrix and other adapted parameters to save time on the adaptation phase, and you could intialise parameter values using the samples from the full posterior samples, but still you could save less than 50% time. And I think it's not yet possible to skip the adaptation yet.
>
> So my suggestion is to run several shorter chains for each cv-fold. Shorter warm-up should be enough if you initialise the parameters for each run from the full posterior samples (different values for each chain)
>
> Aki

messages.body_plain:
Surprising (the result, not that Michael's right about calc!).
It looks like we're optimizing f in one case and h in the second,
where

  f(y_raw, mu, sigma,theta) = g(sigma * y_raw + mu, mu, sigma, theta)
                               + log normal(y_raw | 0, 1)

vs.

  h(y, mu, sigma, theta) = g(y, mu, sigma, theta)
                           + log normal(y | mu, sigma)

                         = g(y, mu, sigma, theta)
                           + log normal((y - mu)/sigma | 0, 1)
                           - log(sigma)

where g is just the rest of the model log density.
The only difference is the -log(sigma) term, but that will
cause different densities.

If I did the algebra right, this should go in the manual.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Sometimes people write in with comments about the speed of Stan in particular examples.  Does everyone know that rstan (and, I think, the other versions of Stan) can be configured so it runs in parallel by default?  My laptop has 4 processors and when I run Stan from R, it automatically runs 4 chains, one in each processor.  This makes a big difference!

In Rstan:
library("rstan")
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

Anyway, probably most of you know this, but just in case you don’t . . . you want to do this.  A factor of 4 is nothing to scoff at!

A

messages.subject: How to check if a matrix is positive definite or not
messages.subject_clean: How to check if a matrix is positive definite or not
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm in a process of building a large spatial covariance matrix with lots of blocks. There is a correlation parameter (\gamma) for the off diagonal blocks which need to be constrained such that the resulting covariance matrix is positive definite.

Unfortunately, there is no closed form to get the support of \gamma to ensure the positive definiteness. The support is between -1 and 1 with holes inside. What I did in R is during the sampling, if non-positive definiteness is found (catch the error message from a Cholesky decomposition), I will set the joint log density to the smallest number in log scale (i.e. zero density). Then that proposed \gamma will be declined and keep the previous \gamma.

I'm interested in implementing my model in Rstan to check my own coding (it's so easy to make some small bugs when programming my sampling procedure with such a complicated model, and the convergence is not good so far). But I got stuck when dealing with theses issues.

1. I notice that I can calculate the eigenvalues of a matrix and then check if all positive( or simply the first one, since it's been ordered). But I'm wondering if there be some machine error going on if I'm using this method.

2. Also, if I find a good way to check positive definiteness, is there a way for me to set the joint density to 0 (let stan stay with the previous sample and move on)? Or do I have other ways to address my unknown support issue?

Thanks,

Jiang

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, May 12, 2016 at 4:25:29 PM UTC-4, Jiang Du wrote:

> Unfortunately, there is no closed form to get the support of \gamma to ensure the positive definiteness. The support is between -1 and 1 with holes inside.

In cases like these, the prior often does not integrate to a constant over the support. If it does integrate to a constant, then you could just declare the thing as a cov_matrix in transformed parameters and it will reject any indefinite ones (at considerable cost to the efficiency). If it doesn't integrate to a constant, then you are not drawing from a well-defined posterior distribution.

messages.subject: statistics for science course with STAN
messages.subject_clean: statistics for science course with STAN
messages.body_plain:
I had an opportunity to teach a course titled 'Statistics for Science' this semester (24 undergraduates, mostly juniors and seniors, 50% computer science/engineering majors with a few math, environmental science, and bio majors).   Topics included the usual survey of estimation and linear models (regression, ANOVA, ANCOVA).

I decided to take a chance and go all in with STAN (via rstan) as the default software and Bayesian as the dominant paradigm (despite the fact that I was trained as a frequentist in the 1970's).

Students used their own computers (65% mac, the rest windows).  Aside from a few headaches getting things to run on windows (which the CS students took as a challenge and for the most part quickly resolved) everything worked great and students generally liked the course.

I think this audience would have tuned out a more traditional approach very quickly.

Thank you for STAN!

messages.subject: VB memory usage issue
messages.subject_clean: VB memory usage issue
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I've been working with a relatively simple categorical model in Stan, but due to its size I've been using variational inference through vb. The inference seems to complete: it gets to the "returning 1000 approximate samples from the posterior" stage and then prints "COMPLETED." However, before control is returned back to me, memory usage spikes to using all available system memory and effectively hangs my system.

What I'm wondering is: what is happening in this stage and is there any way to deal with the memory spike through some parameters? Can someone who knows the inner workings of the vb call explain what it's doing after ostensibly finishing sampling from the posterior that would cause such a massive consumption of memory?

Thanks,
Rick

messages.subject_clean: Random Walk Metropolis for general manifolds
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

This question is a bit theoretical in nature, so forgive me.

I was wondering - does Random Walk Metropolis work as it does in R_n for manifolds? For example, if we had a von Mises distribution on the sphere, does it work? (I am assuming we are able to determine geodesics on the manifold, and use these to generate dependent samples.)

I have been searching for a while, and can't seem to find the answer to this definitively; I see lots of papers on generalising HMC to manifolds, but haven't seen simple Random Walk Metropolis. The reason for considering the latter is that I am looking at solving an (somewhat expensive) integral equation on the surface of the manifold, and I am just not sure how easy it will be to calculate its derivatives in a reasonable amount of time.

Best,

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Fitting an ODE time course in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Having time-dependent forcing terms, dx/dt = I(t) + g(x) is in general
not an issue for integrate_ode.  If you know a functional form for
I(t) then you just add it to the ODE functor specification.  If I(t) is
piecewise constant then you can recreate that using if/then statements
in the ODE functor specification.

Alternatively you can call integrate_ode only over the periods for
which I(t) is constant, instead of trying to integrate over many points
at once.

You would have to implement the ODE this way no matter where
you build your analysis, so moving to Python or Julia (or, gulp,
trying to get away with an Euler integrator) isn’t going to make
that any easier than building it in Stan.  Plus you’d immediately
loose the scalable MCMC and be introducing even worse problems.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Random Walk Metropolis for general manifolds
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Random Walk Metropolis for general manifolds
messages.body_plain:
Firstly, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is defined on manifolds, it does not
have to be “generalized to manifolds”.  It’s geometric by construction.

Metropolis-Hastings works on arbitrary state spaces, and hence is
fine for manifolds.  The problem is trying to construct a proposal
mechanism that stays on the manifold, which is _very_ hard to do
in general.  If you can construct geodesics then you can emulate
Random Walk by choosing a random direction and flowing along
the geodesic for epsilon time, but otherwise you’d need gradient
information to construct a proper path through the manifold.

And that's why there are whole branches of literature devoted
to things like "generating random correlation matrices".

Luckily, it's pretty easy for spheres --- probably why they're
always the first example of non-trivial manifolds.

There's a nice duality between generating random X-es, having
constrained variables that are Xs, and writing densities over Xs.
This is how Ben created the LKJ density out of Lewandowski, Kurowicka,
and Joe's method for generating correlation matrices.

Stan lets you do this automatically for simplexes, ordered
vectors, unit vectors (coming in Stan 2.10), correlation matrices,
and covariance matrices, as well as Cholesky factors of correlation
or covariance matrices.  It's just a mass of constraining transforms
and Jacobian calculations (all described in the manual chapter on
transforms/constraints).

- Bob

messages.subject: Include stateline capabilities in Stan?
messages.subject_clean: Include stateline capabilities in Stan?
messages.body_plain:
There's a distributed MCMC software called stateline (https://github.com/NICTA/stateline) which implements random walk Metropolis-Hastings with parallel tempering. It claims to improve chain mixing and to provide an adaptive proposal distribution to speed up convergence, and allows the user to factorise their likelihoods (eg. over sensors or data). While that may be great I would love to have to opportunity of using the NUTS sampling algorithm in that framework.

The biggest benefit would be to distribute several hundreds of chains easily through a server running on a high powered cluster. Think, 100's of users submitting chains to this server architecture running chains for their simulations. That would really kick some serious ass in my optics.

Anyone has any experience with this or heard of any plans to join Stan and Statline attempts? To me it seems like a match made in heaven.

Best,
Michael

messages.subject: Overestimated standard deviation (SD)
messages.subject_clean: Overestimated standard deviation (SD)
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

down votefavorite <http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/212722/overestimated-mcmc-standard-deviation-sd#>

I did a simulation study with 100 replications for a complex model with rstan, and I found the standard deviation (SD) of posterior samples is larger than the true value. This seems to depend on the number of chains.

The idea is that, I simulated 100 data sets from a model. For each data set, I fit it with rstan, and I save the point estimate (of β) and standard deviation of the posterior samples in est_b and sd_brespectively. So est_b and sd_b are both a vector of 100 elements.

If I use the default setting (chains = 4, iter = 2000) in rstan, the average calculated SD in a single replication (mean(sd_b)) is higher than the true SD (sd(est_b), SD of 100 point estimates, we treated this as the true value of SD).
> mean(sd_b)
[1] 0.4838592
> sd(est_b)
[1] 0.4376797

If I use only 1 chain but iter = 4*2000, the two metrics seem similar.
> mean(sd_b)
[1] 0.4740169
> sd(est_b)
[1] 0.4712312

I also tried 8 chains but got similar result as 4 chains. I am wondering if anyone has confronted this kind of problem before, or has an explanation / solution for this, and I am also not sure if this issue is Stan specific. I can share the code and data if an reproducible example is needed.

Thanks a lot,
Randel

messages.body_plain:
real[] onecomp_mm_infusion(real t, real[] y, real[] theta, real[] x_r, int[] x_i) {
  real dydt[1];

  if (t < x_r[2])
    dydt[1] <- - theta[2] * y[1] / ( theta[1] * (theta[3] + y[1]) ) + x_r[1] / (theta[1] * x_r[2]);
  else
    dydt[1] <- - theta[2] * y[1] / ( theta[1] * (theta[3] + y[1]) );

  return dydt;

}

I've received some excellent help from this list, and now that my code is working - I need to get it to run more quickly. I have read a lot about vectorizing and I've looked up some examples, but I'm having difficulty vectorizing loops like what follows:

for (p in 1:P) {
   mup[p] ~ normal(mum[imodel[p]] + if_else(kc1[p], bkc1,  noval) + if_else(kc2[p], bkc2, noval) + if_else(kc3[p], bkc3, noval) + if_else(kc4[p],
                            bkc4, noval), sigmap[p]);
    }

I thought that I should be able to do something like the following:

   mup[p] ~ normal(mum[imodel] + if_else(kc1, bkc1,  noval) + if_else(kc2, bkc2, noval) + if_else(kc3, bkc3, noval) + if_else(kc3,
                            bkc4, noval), sigmap);

But I received several error messages about ill-formed equations.

The above mup[p] follows a normal distribution with a mean vector that contains an intercept (this is a hierarchical construction) and a number of fixed effects (so I've used the if_else construction as opposed to multiplying matrices).

Right now, mup, kc1-4, and sigmap are all defined similarly, P-length vectors, e.g. vector [P] mup;. and bkc1-4 are defined as real values, and "noval" is transformed data, because when I simply had "0" in the same place, I received an error message that the quantity had to be a real number, so noval (no value) is defined as real, and is equal to zero.

Any suggestions for how to vectorize this would be greatly appreciated. I can't seem to find an example that I can work from - though maybe that's because I don't know what I'm looking for?

Thank you so much.

Shauna

messages.body_plain:
Will do:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1868#issuecomment-219460909

I'll try to add this discussion:

Efficiency involves two issues in Stan, and both stem
from first principles:

1.  Statistical Efficiency.  This is all about posterior curvature
in Stan.  Some posteriors are easy to move around than others and
changing parameterizations can help.
(This is also true of Gibbs and Metropolis, by the way.)

2.  Computational Efficiency.  This is all about efficient
derivatives, and the smaller the resulting expression graph,
the faster the derivatives.  That's why vectorization involving
parameters gives you an efficiency boost but vectorization of
constants doesn't.

The if_else stems from point 2 --- there are fewer terms in
the expression graph for the if_else.   But there's a catch.
The if_else evaluates both sides, so in general, a conditional
is required, so instead of

  a <- a + if_else(cond, b, c)

where b and c are complex expressions, it's more efficient
to do this

  if (cond)
    a <- a + b;
  else
    a <- a + c;

We're adding a ternary operation that'll avoid the eager evaluation
of the RHS terms.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Random Walk Metropolis for general manifolds
messages.body_plain:
The unit vectors for spheres use the overparameterization
plus prior trick (C^{n} embedded in R^{n+1}).  Not an isomorphism,
but it should have better locality for things like wrapping
than the R^{n} version.

- Bob

> On May 14, 2016, at 12:27 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Note that this duality is possible only for spaces
> isomorphic to R^{n}, so wouldn’t work for spheres
> or PSD matrices, etc, which are nontrivial manifolds.
>
> On May 14, 2016, at 5:07 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
>> And that's why there are whole branches of literature devoted
>> to things like "generating random correlation matrices".
>>
>> Luckily, it's pretty easy for spheres --- probably why they're
>> always the first example of non-trivial manifolds.
>>
>> There's a nice duality between generating random X-es, having
>> constrained variables that are Xs, and writing densities over Xs.
>> This is how Ben created the LKJ density out of Lewandowski, Kurowicka,
>> and Joe's method for generating correlation matrices.
>>
>> Stan lets you do this automatically for simplexes, ordered
>> vectors, unit vectors (coming in Stan 2.10), correlation matrices,
>> and covariance matrices, as well as Cholesky factors of correlation
>> or covariance matrices.  It's just a mass of constraining transforms
>> and Jacobian calculations (all described in the manual chapter on
>> transforms/constraints).
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>

>>>
>>> Firstly, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is defined on manifolds, it does not
>>> have to be “generalized to manifolds”.  It’s geometric by construction.
>>>
>>> Metropolis-Hastings works on arbitrary state spaces, and hence is
>>> fine for manifolds.  The problem is trying to construct a proposal

A[i:j, k:l] <- B; // i,j,k,l integers

that weren't previously possible. Hope that helps,

Jonah

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question about vectorizing
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Question about vectorizing
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, May 16, 2016 at 11:09:52 AM UTC-4, Shauna Sweet wrote:
> So if I understand your suggestion fully: I should retain the loop, but within the model statement I should separate the calculation of the mean of the mean (which includes a grand mean of sorts and also a series of fixed effects), from the specification of the distribution of that mean.

In this case, yes. You don't need to do that if the calculation of the mean of the mean can itself be vectorized easily,
but in your case you'll probably need to do that if you want to vectorize. If I understand your situation correctly then
you'll want to get it into the form

mup ~ normal(mup_mean, mup_sd),

where mup_mean is a vector/array of means and mup_sd is a vector/array of standard deviations (of the same length as mup_mean).
If you have to construct those vectors in a loop that's fine as long as the call to normal is vectorized (that's where the real speedup is).

Hope that helps,

messages.body_plain:
Hi, I have 3 thoughts. First, yes, subset the data for sure.  We have ideas of how to do this more formally (see here: http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/ep.pdf), but even a simple partitioning will often make sense.  Second, strip down your model.  Remove most of these varying intercepts. Start with a model with only one of these sigmas.  That should run fast.  Then add them, one at a time, and see how that goes.
Third, once you start to add in these factors, start by giving them fixed values of sigma.  For example, sigma=0.1 or 0.2.  Remember, excluding a factor is just sigma=0.  In lots of these examples, these sigmas aren't so well identified anyway.  Run the models with fixed sigmas, that should be fast.  In fact, with fixed sigmas this is just a logistic regression model with a prior, you could even do point estimation, perhaps.  Then replaces some of the fixed sigmas with priors, etc.  Build up to it.  Ideally the entire process should just take a few days.

10 iterations a day is ridiculous:  there's no way you should trust your model enough to sit around and wait like that.  I'd have more confidence in a model with externally-supplied sigmas that could run fast so you could try out different possibilities.

Also this example could be a good candidate for GMO, perhaps.

A

messages.body_plain:
Just as an additional comment to such ODEs: The ODE RHS function is discontinuous at t=x_r[2] as there is a sudden change. The integrated function itself is still continuous, but the ODE RHS is not. The latter is somewhat problematic for any integrator (ODE integrator always assume continuity of the integrator function and the integrated RHS) and one should work around it by stopping and restarting the integration there. So we want to integrate from t0 < tmid = x_r[2] < tend such a function with initial y0 at t0, then what is ideal to do is to run two commands of integrate_ode as:

part1 = integrate_ode(ode_rhs, t0, y0, ts1, ...); with ts1 = (... tmid), tmid is the n1'th time-point

then we do

part2 = integrate_ode(ode_rhs, tmid, part1[n1], ts2, ...); with ts2 = (one-after-tmid, ... tend)

That's it. Now the ODE RHS is always continuous when given to the integrator. Not doing this will likely work, but the solution won't be precise around the discontinuity and the integrator will be inefficient in that region as the step-size will be decreased to very small values.

Sebastian

Double exponential is a proper desnity, so it doesn't have
flat tails.

Yes, you can define a covariance matrix in transformed parameters
that has some zero elements and some varying elements.  Maintaining
positive-definiteness is the tricky part.  You don't want to just
be rejecting because HMC will reduce to a very inefficient rejection
sampler.

> See this example for a daily seasonality http://tjo-en.hatenablog.com/entry/2015/08/18/123000

Thanks for linking to the blog (love your icon, by the way).

In the linked blog entry, you want to make sure you use <lower=0> with
all of your scale parameters (s_trend, etc.) --- they need to be > 0.

I didn't understand why you set the model up the way you did.  But
this

  season[i]~normal(-season[i-1]
                   - season[i-2]
                   - season[i-3]
                   - season[i-4]
                   - season[i-5]
                   - season[i-6], s_season);

is more efficiently (and compactly) coded as:

  season[i] ~ normal(-sum(season[(i-6):(i-1)]), s_season);

And if you declare your variables as vectors rather than arrays, you can
vectorize this

  for (i in 1:N)
    q[i]~normal(a*x1[i]+b*x2[i]+c*x3[i]+d,s_q);

as

  q ~ normal(a * x1 + b * x2 + c * x3 + d, s_q);

That should help quite a bit with speed.

- Bob

      on different platforms.

messages.subject: Stan parallel works in Windows 10
messages.subject_clean: Stan parallel works in Windows 10
messages.body_plain:
This may be old news, but it seems to me that Rstan (at least on Windows 10 on my 2-core laptop) is capable of running parallel chains in Windows without any extra programming effort (e.g., setting up a cluster for parLapply). Stan now launches additional R processes and redirects output to the "Viewer" in Rstudio merely by setting the cores=x option. Maybe this feature was added at some point, but I don't see it anywhere in the Rstan docs (?).

I am posting this merely so that other users of Windows who don't ever bother with parLapply but enjoy the ease of parallel usage with mclapply, etc. on Linux/Mac, can go ahead and use Rstan in parallel without any worries.

Note, though, that using the default Rstan detect_cores() option on Windows will report "logical cores", which are not true hardware cores. You can find out the true number of cores on a Windows 10 machine by going to Task Manager -> Performance tab. It's not hard on other versions to find the true number of cores. Be sure to then set the cores option in stan() manually to the true number of cores, or running stan() in parallel will slow your machine down considerably.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the heads up on this. So I am not sure I will be able to do that particular method of starting and stopping the integrator with individual parts outside of the integrate_ode function, because I will have an x_r array with tens of thousands of changes (I feel that there are some problems with both the models and the data, but it's just what I have to work with, for now). Definitely anticipating inefficiencies, if having a step-wise forcing function with tens of thousands of discontinuities will even work at all.

On Tuesday, May 17, 2016 at 12:20:14 AM UTC-7, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> Just as an additional comment to such ODEs: The ODE RHS function is discontinuous at t=x_r[2] as there is a sudden change. The integrated function itself is still continuous, but the ODE RHS is not. The latter is somewhat problematic for any integrator (ODE integrator always assume continuity of the integrator function and the integrated RHS) and one should work around it by stopping and restarting the integration there. So we want to integrate from t0 < tmid = x_r[2] < tend such a function with initial y0 at t0, then what is ideal to do is to run two commands of integrate_ode as:
>
> part1 = integrate_ode(ode_rhs, t0, y0, ts1, ...); with ts1 = (... tmid), tmid is the n1'th time-point
>
> then we do
>
> part2 = integrate_ode(ode_rhs, tmid, part1[n1], ts2, ...); with ts2 = (one-after-tmid, ... tend)
>
> That's it. Now the ODE RHS is always continuous when given to the integrator. Not doing this will likely work, but the solution won't be precise around the discontinuity and the integrator will be inefficient in that region as the step-size will be decreased to very small values.
>
> Sebastian
>
> On Sunday, May 15, 2016 at 12:53:28 PM UTC+2, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > real[] onecomp_mm_infusion(real t, real[] y, real[] theta, real[] x_r, int[] x_i) {
> >   real dydt[1];
> >
> >   if (t < x_r[2])
> >     dydt[1] <- - theta[2] * y[1] / ( theta[1] * (theta[3] + y[1]) ) + x_r[1] / (theta[1] * x_r[2]);
> >   else
> >     dydt[1] <- - theta[2] * y[1] / ( theta[1] * (theta[3] + y[1]) );
> >
> >   return dydt;
> > }
> >
> >
> > On May 15, 2016, at 6:57 AM, Hua Xie <yaois...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > > Hi Michael,
> > >
> > > Thanks for your help. I have started out getting the most basic of models working in Stan to learn it, but admittedly am still confused and have not been able to find much in the way of examples with forcing. I actually have multiple forcing terms in my actual mode, some piecewise linear, others for which I have a functional form. Here is a simplified template of the data and model I am working with:
> > >
> > > int N //Where N = 40. My data is sampled on 50 days over a 500 day interval
> > > real C[N] //Time course data I am trying to fit
> > > real I[N] //Data for input forcing piecewise constant function that changes with every new N.
> > > real Z[T] //Forcing for which I have functional form. Let's say Z[T] = sin(T).
> > >
> > > dX/dT = I - theta[1] * X + theta[2] * Y / Z * (1 + X + Y)
> > > dY/dT = -theta[3] * Y + theta[4] * X / Z * (1 + X + Y)
> > >
> > > Chat[N] = (1 - theta[1]) * X[N]
> > >
> > > C[N] ~ normal(Chat[N],sigma)
> > >
> > > If you can offer me some guidance and clarification in terms of Stan pseudocode, I would really appreciate it. What would my ODE function block and integrate_ode statement look like with a piecewise constant function? Is this where I would use the x_r variable?
> > >
> > > Thank you.
> > >
> > > On Saturday, May 14, 2016 at 1:45:54 AM UTC-7, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > > Having time-dependent forcing terms, dx/dt = I(t) + g(x) is in general
> > > not an issue for integrate_ode.  If you know a functional form for
> > > I(t) then you just add it to the ODE functor specification.  If I(t) is
> > > piecewise constant then you can recreate that using if/then statements
> > > in the ODE functor specification.
> > >
> > > Alternatively you can call integrate_ode only over the periods for
> > > which I(t) is constant, instead of trying to integrate over many points
> > > at once.
> > >
> > > You would have to implement the ODE this way no matter where
> > > you build your analysis, so moving to Python or Julia (or, gulp,
> > > trying to get away with an Euler integrator) isn’t going to make
> > > that any easier than building it in Stan.  Plus you’d immediately
> > > loose the scalable MCMC and be introducing even worse problems.
> > >
> > > On May 14, 2016, at 2:57 AM, Hua Xie <yaois...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > >> I recently find out about several changes to a project I am working on in graduate school, and rather than fitting a vector of stable ODE solutions, I am now trying to fit time courses for which some input data is changing at every time step in my equations, i.e. for a dx/dt = I + g(x), I is changing at every dt. Actual model is a lot more complex than that, of course.
> > >>
> > >> I am figuring out the best way of doing this, as I will not be able to use integrate_ode for my purposes because of the transient input data. I am debating between coding my entire script in Python/Julia with a simple Metropolis-Hastings MCMC algorithm for parameter fitting, trying out PyMC, or doing a simple Euler in Stan and still taking advantage of Stan's HMC. I just wanted to see if people had some success stories/example code of coding their own simple ODE solvers in Stan.

messages.body_plain:
One more question --
So the ODE equations are on an hourly scale. One of the input terms changes every hour. My original plan was to have something like
dydt <- x_r[iceil(t)] - etc. However, Stan does not seem to have a ceiling/floor function that returns integers, last I checked. Is there an alternative to using a ceiling/floor function that comes to mind?

Thanks

On Tuesday, May 17, 2016 at 4:20:10 PM UTC-7, Hua Xie wrote:
> Thanks for the heads up on this. So I am not sure I will be able to do that particular method of starting and stopping the integrator with individual parts outside of the integrate_ode function, because I will have an x_r array with tens of thousands of changes (I feel that there are some problems with both the models and the data, but it's just what I have to work with, for now). Definitely anticipating inefficiencies, if having a step-wise forcing function with tens of thousands of discontinuities will even work at all.
>
> On Tuesday, May 17, 2016 at 12:20:14 AM UTC-7, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> > Just as an additional comment to such ODEs: The ODE RHS function is discontinuous at t=x_r[2] as there is a sudden change. The integrated function itself is still continuous, but the ODE RHS is not. The latter is somewhat problematic for any integrator (ODE integrator always assume continuity of the integrator function and the integrated RHS) and one should work around it by stopping and restarting the integration there. So we want to integrate from t0 < tmid = x_r[2] < tend such a function with initial y0 at t0, then what is ideal to do is to run two commands of integrate_ode as:
> >
> > part1 = integrate_ode(ode_rhs, t0, y0, ts1, ...); with ts1 = (... tmid), tmid is the n1'th time-point
> >
> > then we do
> >
> > part2 = integrate_ode(ode_rhs, tmid, part1[n1], ts2, ...); with ts2 = (one-after-tmid, ... tend)
> >
> > That's it. Now the ODE RHS is always continuous when given to the integrator. Not doing this will likely work, but the solution won't be precise around the discontinuity and the integrator will be inefficient in that region as the step-size will be decreased to very small values.
> >
> > Sebastian
> >
> > On Sunday, May 15, 2016 at 12:53:28 PM UTC+2, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > > real[] onecomp_mm_infusion(real t, real[] y, real[] theta, real[] x_r, int[] x_i) {
> > >   real dydt[1];
> > >
> > >   if (t < x_r[2])
> > >     dydt[1] <- - theta[2] * y[1] / ( theta[1] * (theta[3] + y[1]) ) + x_r[1] / (theta[1] * x_r[2]);
> > >   else
> > >     dydt[1] <- - theta[2] * y[1] / ( theta[1] * (theta[3] + y[1]) );
> > >
> > >   return dydt;
> > > }
> > >
> > >
> > > On May 15, 2016, at 6:57 AM, Hua Xie <yaois...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > > Hi Michael,
> > > >
> > > > Thanks for your help. I have started out getting the most basic of models working in Stan to learn it, but admittedly am still confused and have not been able to find much in the way of examples with forcing. I actually have multiple forcing terms in my actual mode, some piecewise linear, others for which I have a functional form. Here is a simplified template of the data and model I am working with:
> > > >
> > > > int N //Where N = 40. My data is sampled on 50 days over a 500 day interval
> > > > real C[N] //Time course data I am trying to fit
> > > > real I[N] //Data for input forcing piecewise constant function that changes with every new N.
> > > > real Z[T] //Forcing for which I have functional form. Let's say Z[T] = sin(T).
> > > >
> > > > dX/dT = I - theta[1] * X + theta[2] * Y / Z * (1 + X + Y)
> > > > dY/dT = -theta[3] * Y + theta[4] * X / Z * (1 + X + Y)
> > > >
> > > > Chat[N] = (1 - theta[1]) * X[N]
> > > >
> > > > C[N] ~ normal(Chat[N],sigma)
> > > >
> > > > If you can offer me some guidance and clarification in terms of Stan pseudocode, I would really appreciate it. What would my ODE function block and integrate_ode statement look like with a piecewise constant function? Is this where I would use the x_r variable?
> > > >
> > > > Thank you.
> > > >
> > > > On Saturday, May 14, 2016 at 1:45:54 AM UTC-7, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > > > Having time-dependent forcing terms, dx/dt = I(t) + g(x) is in general
> > > > not an issue for integrate_ode.  If you know a functional form for
> > > > I(t) then you just add it to the ODE functor specification.  If I(t) is
> > > > piecewise constant then you can recreate that using if/then statements
> > > > in the ODE functor specification.
> > > >
> > > > Alternatively you can call integrate_ode only over the periods for
> > > > which I(t) is constant, instead of trying to integrate over many points
> > > > at once.
> > > >
> > > > You would have to implement the ODE this way no matter where
> > > > you build your analysis, so moving to Python or Julia (or, gulp,
> > > > trying to get away with an Euler integrator) isn’t going to make
> > > > that any easier than building it in Stan.  Plus you’d immediately
> > > > loose the scalable MCMC and be introducing even worse problems.
> > > >

messages.subject: What determines the convergence rate of ADVI?
messages.subject_clean: What determines the convergence rate of ADVI?
messages.body_plain:
For quasi-HMC MCMC stamping (eg NUTS algorithm used in STAN), the rate of convergence is roughly determined by the geometry of the posterior, and in particular:
The degree of posterior correlation - high posterior correlations degrade the performance of the sampler if a dense mass matrix is not used,
The skewness of the posterior - (eg things which look like bananas will be hard to sample from without a non-Euclidean mass matrix), and
The kurtosis of the posterior - heavy tailed posteriors are hard to sample from.

What determines the speed of ADVI convergence using the stochastic gradient descent algorithm?

I presume that the primary factors are the same, and in particular the extent to which different directions have different scales - gradient descent performs poorly if the scales of different parameters vary greatly.

Does heavy tailedness have an impact given that this is an optimisation algorithm?

Thanks

> > > Just as an additional comment to such ODEs: The ODE RHS function is discontinuous at t=x_r[2] as there is a sudden change. The integrated function itself is still continuous, but the ODE RHS is not. The latter is somewhat problematic for any integrator (ODE integrator always assume continuity of the integrator function and the integrated RHS) and one should work around it by stopping and restarting the integration there. So we want to integrate from t0 < tmid = x_r[2] < tend such a function with initial y0 at t0, then what is ideal to do is to run two commands of integrate_ode as:
> > >
> > > part1 = integrate_ode(ode_rhs, t0, y0, ts1, ...); with ts1 = (... tmid), tmid is the n1'th time-point
> > >
> > > then we do
> > >
> > > part2 = integrate_ode(ode_rhs, tmid, part1[n1], ts2, ...); with ts2 = (one-after-tmid, ... tend)
> > >
> > > That's it. Now the ODE RHS is always continuous when given to the integrator. Not doing this will likely work, but the solution won't be precise around the discontinuity and the integrator will be inefficient in that region as the step-size will be decreased to very small values.

messages.body_plain:
Yes, I would personally love to replace it with a continuous approximation of the forcing function. However, my supervisor still wants to fit the discontinuous data, and have been unable to convince him otherwise. I will continue discussing that with him -- in the mean time, is there any way to code what I described?

Thanks again for your patient help, Sebastian.

On Wed, May 18, 2016 at 1:10 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:

> No, there is no ceiling function in Stan. Given your forcing function is that flexible and changing so often... maybe replace that with a spline or something else which is a continuous approximation to that forcing function?
>
> The problem you describe sounds like you will have to think about how to make it easier to fit, i.e. approximate somehow and simplify.
>
> Sebastian
>
>
> On Wednesday, May 18, 2016 at 3:08:18 AM UTC+2, Hua Xie wrote:
> > One more question --
> > So the ODE equations are on an hourly scale. One of the input terms changes every hour. My original plan was to have something like
> > dydt <- x_r[iceil(t)] - etc. However, Stan does not seem to have a ceiling/floor function that returns integers, last I checked. Is there an alternative to using a ceiling/floor function that comes to mind?
> >
> > Thanks
> >
> > On Tuesday, May 17, 2016 at 4:20:10 PM UTC-7, Hua Xie wrote:
> > > Thanks for the heads up on this. So I am not sure I will be able to do that particular method of starting and stopping the integrator with individual parts outside of the integrate_ode function, because I will have an x_r array with tens of thousands of changes (I feel that there are some problems with both the models and the data, but it's just what I have to work with, for now). Definitely anticipating inefficiencies, if having a step-wise forcing function with tens of thousands of discontinuities will even work at all.
> > >
> > > On Tuesday, May 17, 2016 at 12:20:14 AM UTC-7, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> > > > Just as an additional comment to such ODEs: The ODE RHS function is discontinuous at t=x_r[2] as there is a sudden change. The integrated function itself is still continuous, but the ODE RHS is not. The latter is somewhat problematic for any integrator (ODE integrator always assume continuity of the integrator function and the integrated RHS) and one should work around it by stopping and restarting the integration there. So we want to integrate from t0 < tmid = x_r[2] < tend such a function with initial y0 at t0, then what is ideal to do is to run two commands of integrate_ode as:
> > > >
> > > > part1 = integrate_ode(ode_rhs, t0, y0, ts1, ...); with ts1 = (... tmid), tmid is the n1'th time-point
> > > >
> > > > then we do
> > > >
> > > > part2 = integrate_ode(ode_rhs, tmid, part1[n1], ts2, ...); with ts2 = (one-after-tmid, ... tend)
> > > >
> > > > That's it. Now the ODE RHS is always continuous when given to the integrator. Not doing this will likely work, but the solution won't be precise around the discontinuity and the integrator will be inefficient in that region as the step-size will be decreased to very small values.
> > > >
> > > > Sebastian
> > > >
> > > > On Sunday, May 15, 2016 at 12:53:28 PM UTC+2, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > > > > real[] onecomp_mm_infusion(real t, real[] y, real[] theta, real[] x_r, int[] x_i) {
> > > > >   real dydt[1];
> > > > >
> > > > >   if (t < x_r[2])
> > > > >     dydt[1] <- - theta[2] * y[1] / ( theta[1] * (theta[3] + y[1]) ) + x_r[1] / (theta[1] * x_r[2]);
> > > > >   else
> > > > >     dydt[1] <- - theta[2] * y[1] / ( theta[1] * (theta[3] + y[1]) );
> > > > >
> > > > >   return dydt;
> > > > > }
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On May 15, 2016, at 6:57 AM, Hua Xie <yaois...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > > Hi Michael,
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Thanks for your help. I have started out getting the most basic of models working in Stan to learn it, but admittedly am still confused and have not been able to find much in the way of examples with forcing. I actually have multiple forcing terms in my actual mode, some piecewise linear, others for which I have a functional form. Here is a simplified template of the data and model I am working with:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > int N //Where N = 40. My data is sampled on 50 days over a 500 day interval
> > > > > > real C[N] //Time course data I am trying to fit
> > > > > > real I[N] //Data for input forcing piecewise constant function that changes with every new N.
> > > > > > real Z[T] //Forcing for which I have functional form. Let's say Z[T] = sin(T).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > dX/dT = I - theta[1] * X + theta[2] * Y / Z * (1 + X + Y)
> > > > > > dY/dT = -theta[3] * Y + theta[4] * X / Z * (1 + X + Y)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Chat[N] = (1 - theta[1]) * X[N]
> > > > > >
> > > > > > C[N] ~ normal(Chat[N],sigma)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > If you can offer me some guidance and clarification in terms of Stan pseudocode, I would really appreciate it. What would my ODE function block and integrate_ode statement look like with a piecewise constant function? Is this where I would use the x_r variable?
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Thank you.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Saturday, May 14, 2016 at 1:45:54 AM UTC-7, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > > > > > Having time-dependent forcing terms, dx/dt = I(t) + g(x) is in general
> > > > > > not an issue for integrate_ode.  If you know a functional form for
> > > > > > I(t) then you just add it to the ODE functor specification.  If I(t) is
> > > > > > piecewise constant then you can recreate that using if/then statements
> > > > > > in the ODE functor specification.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Alternatively you can call integrate_ode only over the periods for
> > > > > > which I(t) is constant, instead of trying to integrate over many points
> > > > > > at once.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > You would have to implement the ODE this way no matter where
> > > > > > you build your analysis, so moving to Python or Julia (or, gulp,
> > > > > > trying to get away with an Euler integrator) isn’t going to make
> > > > > > that any easier than building it in Stan.  Plus you’d immediately
> > > > > > loose the scalable MCMC and be introducing even worse problems.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On May 14, 2016, at 2:57 AM, Hua Xie <yaois...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > >
> > > > > >> I recently find out about several changes to a project I am working on in graduate school, and rather than fitting a vector of stable ODE solutions, I am now trying to fit time courses for which some input data is changing at every time step in my equations, i.e. for a dx/dt = I + g(x), I is changing at every dt. Actual model is a lot more complex than that, of course.
> > > > > >>
> > > > > >> I am figuring out the best way of doing this, as I will not be able to use integrate_ode for my purposes because of the transient input data. I am debating between coding my entire script in Python/Julia with a simple Metropolis-Hastings MCMC algorithm for parameter fitting, trying out PyMC, or doing a simple Euler in Stan and still taking advantage of Stan's HMC. I just wanted to see if people had some success stories/example code of coding their own simple ODE solvers in Stan.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Normal Distribution ordered or not?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Normal Distribution ordered or not?
messages.body_plain:
I didn't understand your I notation --- is that a carryover
for BUGS/JAGS that's missing a comma?

What this

> ordered[K] b[J];

does is make sure that b[j,1] < b[j,2] < ... < b[j,K]
for all j.  And it gets an implicit improper uniform prior
over all b meeting the constraint.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Given some subject specific parameters theta_i ~ N(mu,sd)
If I assume a uniform hyperprior for mu, is there any need to assign it as a parameter to sample?
Or can I just as well treat theta_i ~ N(mean(theta),sd)

The latter approach seems to be working more efficiently for me than either a centered or non-centered parameterization of theta_i, and I haven't been able to come up with any negatives, aside from the uniform prior restriction which I don't find problematic so far.

For a start, it doesn't define a proper density because
the following doesn't evaluate to 1

  INTEGRAL_Theta p(theta | sd) d.theta

  = INTEGRAL_Theta PROD_i normal(theta[i] | mean(theta), sd) d.theta

This is easy to see because p(theta | y) = p(theta + c | y)
for any c, so there's an infinite-mass ridge as discussed in
the problematic posteriors chapter of the manual.

messages.subject: Two dependent variables, imputations, and LOO
messages.subject_clean: Two dependent variables, imputations, and LOO
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan,

First of all, thank you so much to the Stan team for this wonderful piece of software. It's been invaluable to my lab so far.

I've been modelling a decision making task in which participants must decide to accept or reject an offer with varying risk and reward features. So far, we have been incorporating both choice and reaction time data to estimate parameters of the model. Choice data is fit using a logistic regression, whereas reaction time is fit through a linear regression. To achieve this, we infer a per-trial likelihood-of-take, theta, from the logistic regression; then we compute d=(theta - 0.5)^2 to estimate the distance of that trial from that participant's point of maximal decision conflict. The resulting d values are linearly regressed against the reaction time, with the assumption that reaction times increase as participants experience more decision conflict.

All of that being said, we are interested in using LOO for model comparison purposes. I am struggling with the following two questions in computing the log-likelihood:

1)  Because we have two dependent variables, is it appropriate to sum across the two log-likelihoods, choice and reaction time, per trial seeing as they are not independent?
2) For about 50/2700 trials, we are missing the recorded reaction times due to equipment failure. As such, I am imputing the reaction time for those trials. Should I include the log-likelihood for these trials? If so, should I only include the log-likelihood for the choice (since we only observed the choice)?

I have attached the model code and my best guess at how to structure the generated quantities section. Any input/thoughts would be greatly appreciated. Thanks in advance for your time!

-Sam

a small circle around it, you get a cylinder of infinite mass.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jon,

I am working on a spatial model, but a different one: the Log-Gaussian Cox Process (Point Patterns). I had the following issues in STAN so far:

1). My code works for small data (about 30 locations) without the spatial random effect (which makes it from LGCP just a Poisson process) and recovers regression coefficients correctly.

2). For larger data, presumably because of the size of the covariance matrix, STAN occupies all the memory (127G) and never finishes computing. If you have not too many areas in CAR, this should not be a problem.

I would be grateful myself to hear about the limit size of the covariance matrix that STAN can cope with.

Liza

On Friday, May 20, 2016 at 11:26:49 AM UTC-4, Carsten Schwemmer wrote:
> I would like to use rstanarm rstan for fitting models to survey data and important thing is that I need to use sampling weights. The weights are represented as simple vectors between {0;1} as a column in a dataframe. Is it possible to apply these weights with rstanarm? And if not, is this possible with rstan?

The model-fitting functions in rstanarm take a (almost entirely untested) weights argument. However, utilizing them is essentially un-Bayesian. For model-based approaches, I think it is better to get the posterior distribution of the parameters conditional on the (unweighted) data in the sample and then obtain posterior predictions for the population that the sample was taken from. The posterior_predict() function in rstanarm facilitates this and a similar thing is done by mrp

https://github.com/malecki/mrp

Ben

messages.subject: Re: Hierarchical Multivariate Normal Models for Quantile Estimation: Inference Problems!
messages.subject_clean: Hierarchical Multivariate Normal Models for Quantile Estimation: Inference Problems!
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob (and anyone else reading this),

Sorry for the long radio silence! I'm back working on this problem now. I think we had hit on 2 issues: either there is a bug, or the way I simulated the data didn't actually have the dependence structure that I thought it had (or both). I have worked on the second issue for the moment, being unable to find a bug yet.

Just to re-cap, I'm trying to model K vectors of estimated quantiles from a set of K continuous distributions. I have enough samples from each distribution that I know the estimated quantiles are approximately distributed as a multivariate normal, with a covariance matrix of known form (result from Mosteller 1946 and probably Laplace earlier than that). So within each site, the vector of quantiles has a MVN sampling distribution and I can estimate the relevant covariance matrix of that sampling distribution. Then I want to throw a hierarchical model on top, shrinking these vectors together across sites.

I got the model to recover parameters of test data without the hierarchical part. Now I am having trouble with the hierarchy. The main issue seems to be estimating the parent covariance matrix (Sigma). As far as I can see, this is not something I can test on a simpler model than the one I use here, because without a hierarchical model that has K > 1, this Sigma does not exist / isn't identifiable. However, it should be identifiable from K > 1 draws from the hierarchical model (although it will be noisily estimated).

So I did 2 things: (1) I simulated data from the stan model itself, (2) I simulated data from a continuous univariate K-block hierarchical distribution directly, then estimated the K sets of quantiles, which are then fed into the hierarchical MVN model.

(1) Didn't work at all (although I may have made a mistake). Exactly the same problem arises as before. And the model takes forever to sample. This makes me think I really must have a bug somewhere. The R file for this is the file name that ends in "from stan simulation fix SEs".

(2) Actually works great for K < 10 or so! I tried a few different variances out here and the model works great on all of them. But it did not work at all for large K: the diagonal elements of Sigma are not way too small, equal to the off diagonals (but the model inference is correct for the off diagonals). This kind of weirdness is confusing to me. Any idea what could be happening? The R file for this one is the file name that ends in "v2".

I want to flag something here: The *true* dependency structure in the MVN model is not that clear, because the vectors are ordered. That ordering induces a mechanical positive correlation between draws because if quantile "t" is drawn higher than average, then quantile "t+1" must be more likely to be higher than average in order to be higher than "t". I find that this correlation grows stronger as I increase the variance (diagonal of Sigma) in my test runs, which makes intuitive sense to me since if we get a very extreme high draw of quantile t, it becomes almost certain that t+1 will have to be above average just to preserve the ordering.

I definitely think at least part of the problem with my "simplified" covariance matrix estimation before is that I actually didn't account for this mechanical correlation from the ordered nature of the vector. However, seems like I still have some bug to iron out here as this does not explain the results completely, and the unconstrained covariance matrix is doing well for K < 10 and poorly otherwise.

Any further advice on any angle of this very ugly knot of a problem is much appreciated. Sorry for returning to the thread on a friday afternoon! I won't abandon it again.

Cheers
Rachael

messages.subject: efficient computation with CARs
messages.subject_clean: efficient computation with CARs
messages.body_plain:
Hi.  I may be mis-remembering here, but I think that with spatial autoregression models (including the intrinsic CAR model), you _don't_ have to write the covariance matrix.  Instead, the efficient way to compute is to just write the prior directly, not as a multilvariate normal but as a product of normal densities.  The point is that you can take advantage of the locality of the conditional dependence when writing the joint prior density.

Also, intrinsic CAR model has no hyperparameters, so if you do express the prior using a covariance matrix, you only have to compute that matrix once, in the transformed data block.

I guess we should do an example!

A

messages.body_plain:
I'd suggest trying a non-centered parameterization.
Declare beta_raw as a vector parameter, and give it
density

  beta_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

and then declare and define (either as transformed parameter or local
variable in the model block), a new vector

  beta <- beta_raw * tau + mu;

to use in the regression, or just define it directly as

  y ~ bernoulli_logit(X * (beta_raw * tau + mu));

Also, that prior on tau is very weak, so if you get extreme
values, you might want to make it tighter.

- Bob

Regarding the "generating model" idea, Snijders and Bosker spend a lot of time comparing the "model based" regression coefficient estimates, which are derived from the hierarchical model with the level 2 units included to model the between-stratum variance,  to the "design based" model coefficients which are derived from a model which weights the likelihood function. From my reading there is not an agreed up standard, and if all else fails, the model based estimates correspond better with the Bayesian framework of modeling. IMO

For an analysis to be Bayesian, it has to use the posterior distribution, p(theta|y) proportional to p(theta) p(y|theta).  In this weighted regression procedure, there is no model p(y|theta).  The procedure uses certain computations that are used in Bayesian analysis--it has some Bayesian elements--but it is not truly a Bayesian analysis because there is no model.

> I've been modelling a decision making task in which participants must decide to accept or reject an offer with varying risk and reward features. So far, we have been incorporating both choice and reaction time data to estimate parameters of the model. Choice data is fit using a logistic regression, whereas reaction time is fit through a linear regression. To achieve this, we infer a per-trial likelihood-of-take, theta, from the logistic regression; then we compute d=(theta - 0.5)^2 to estimate the distance of that trial from that participant's point of maximal decision conflict. The resulting d values are linearly regressed against the reaction time, with the assumption that reaction times increase as participants experience more decision conflict.
>

Should I include the log-likelihood for these trials? If so, should I only include the log-likelihood for the choice (since we only observed the choice)?

For estimating the predictive performance you should include only the terms with observations. You could use the other terms for internal model checking (sensitivity etc)

Aki

>

> > #IF I am monitoring alpha_stz and beta_stz, use the raw parameter to sample, just monitor the stz version
> > parameters{
> >   vector[N] alpha;#random effect, MVN prior
> >   real beta;
> >   real<lower=1e-6> sigma2;
> > }
> > transformed parameters{
> >   real alpha_stz;
> >   real beta_stz;
> >   real mean_alpha;
> >   mean_alpha <- mean(alpha)
> >   alpha_stz <- alpha - mean_alpha;
> >   beta_stz <- beta + mean_alpha;
> > }
> > model{
> >   alpha ~  multi_normal_prec(zeros, Tau)#zeros, Tau defined somewhere else
> >   beta ~ normal(1,2)
> >   y ~ normal(alpha+beta, sigma2)
> > }
> > #another way: use the stz version to sample
> > parameters{
> >   vector[N] alpha;#random effect, MVN prior
> >   real beta;
> >   real<lower=1e-6> sigma2;

> >   alpha_stz <- alpha - mean_alpha;
> >
> >   beta ~ normal(1,2)
> >   y ~ normal(alpha_stz+beta_stz, sigma2)
> > }
> >
> >
> > So basically, I have a vector of random effect alpha, for example, a spatial effect, and an intercept, beta. In order to identify these two, I want to add sum-to-zero constraint to alpha. Here are two ways to do it:
> > 1. Don't care about the constraint during the sampling. After get the posterior samples, add the constraint for every iteration of the samples.
> > 2. For every iteration, use the constraint to create local variable, alpha_stz and beta_stz, use these two to calculate the log likelihood.
> >
> > I understand the probability density will be the same in either case, since the sum of alpha and beta will never change. However, there is some difference between these two methods, which I can't describe clearly. What is the correct way doing so?

messages.body_plain:
Since myself and colleagues still don't see the point, I will try to re-phase, but of course ignore if it's getting frustrating! I just wonder if there is a miscommunication.
Given that

p(theta | y ) = ( p(y|theta) p(theta)  )   /  p(y)  with theta~ uniform(-5,5)

is a well behaved model, what is it about the inclusion of a hyperprior on the sd of theta...

p(theta, sd | y ) = ( p(y|theta) p(theta | sd) p(sd) )   /  p(y)  with theta<lower=-5,upper=5> ~ normal(mean(theta),sd) and sd~uniform(0,100)

that apparently causes the integral to diverge to infinity?
This approach is working much more efficiently for dynamic modelling problems, recovering parameters well, and I realised priors on mean(theta) can also be included, so no restriction to uniform (according to the current, apparently invalid, logic!).

messages.body_plain:
On Monday, May 23, 2016 at 8:56:38 AM UTC-4, juliansc...@aol.com wrote:
> I'm fitting multilevel models with ca 25k random effects, using rstanarm. R then simply got stuck. Looking around a bit I saw that stan_glmer returns the variance-covariance matrix of the coefficients ("covmat") element that already with a model fit on a fifth of my data it is 800MB. It seems I don't have not enough RAM for that model fit on the full data. Is there a way to call stan_glmer without producing the covmat? And also, shouldn't most people be ok with just getting the posterior samples?

Most people, yes, but things like the covariance matrix are needed for some post-estimation methods to work the same way as they do with glmer. In this case, we should probably just calculate the covariance among the common parameters. I'll try to fix this before we release a new rstanarm tomorrow.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
But I still don't understand why you're writing such
a non-identified model.

- Bob

> On May 23, 2016, at 10:13 AM, Charles Driver <cdriv...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Since myself and colleagues still don't see the point, I will try to re-phase, but of course ignore if it's getting frustrating! I just wonder if there is a miscommunication.
>
> Given that
> p(theta | y ) = ( p(y|theta) p(theta)  )   /  p(y)  with theta~ uniform(-5,5)
> is a well behaved model,

So far, you've only defined p(theta).  For the model to be
well behaved, INTEGRAL p(theta | y) d.theta has to be finite.

> what is it about the inclusion of a hyperprior on the sd of theta...
> p(theta, sd | y ) = ( p(y|theta) p(theta | sd) p(sd) )   /  p(y)  with theta<lower=-5,upper=5> ~ normal(mean(theta),sd) and sd~uniform(0,100)
> that apparently causes the integral to diverge to infinity?

If theta is bounded to (-5,5) you'll get a normalizable
posterior.

The problem I was referring to is that this term (where theta is an N-vector
and sd > 0),

  p(theta | sd) = PROD_n normal(theta[n] | mean(theta), sd),

is not normalizable in that INTEGRAL p(theta | sd) d.theta = infinity.

If you bound each theta[n] to (-5,5), the integral will be finite.

But I still don't understand what you think p(theta | sd) is saying
about theta conditional on sd.  Maybe it'd help if you fix a sd,
take N=2 and make a 2D plot of theta[1] x theta[n] in (-5,5) vs. density
with a fixed sigma so you can see what the issue is.

We generally don't recommend bounding parameters because it can
cause problems both statistically (truncating and hence underestimating
uncertainty) and computationally (transforms to unconstrained space
stretch the boundaries).

Why not just make theta uniform on (-5,5)^N?  Or normal centered around
0 if you want shrinkage.

- Bob

> This approach is working much more efficiently for dynamic modelling problems, recovering parameters well, and I realised priors on mean(theta) can also be included, so no restriction to uniform (according to the current, apparently invalid, logic!).
>
> On Friday, May 20, 2016 at 12:45:54 AM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> On May 19, 2016, at 6:08 PM, Charles Driver <cdriv...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Ok. Re-read the problematic posterior section, still struggling to see the infinite mass ridge point, if you or anyone wants to take another try it would be very welcome, otherwise maybe something sinks in over coming days... so far as I see the mass of mean(theta) will be determined by the individual theta likelihoods and sd, in much the same way as the mass of a mu sampled from a uniform distribution.
>
> For a proper density p(theta), INTEGRAL p(theta) d.theta = 1.
> You define
>
>   p(theta) = PROD_i normal(theta[i] | mean(theta), sd)
>
> and the integral diverges to infinity.  More intuitively,
> the ridge is a line of constant density, so if you draw
> a small circle around it, you get a cylinder of infinite mass.
>
> - Bob

It is something people did in WinBUGS, but it's going to
be a problem in Stan because the posterior over the parameters
(that is, what's defined in the parameters block) isn't proper.
In particular, the no-U-turn sampler won't make U-turns --- it'll
just keep running.

messages.subject: Two ways of hierarchical pooling (warning it's more of a math discussion, than stan)
messages.subject_clean: Two ways of hierarchical pooling (warning it's more of a math discussion, than stan)
messages.body_plain:
Hey guys,
Sorry if this doesn't belong on this mailing list. I just couldn't find a better place to ask the question

I'm wondering if anyone of you could tell me any real difference and/or advantage to the following two methods of partial pooling in those simple regression models.

1. example.
For each response variable y_k, (where k = (1:N), each k could e.g. be a different school or country), we want to model the effect of data x on the data y_k, by sampling B_k and an intercept B_0. Assuming all y's are related we pool the B_k towards each other by sampling the mean of each B_k from the same hyper prior. Thus the sigma in b) says how much each B_k are allowed to vary from each other but the sigma_hat in c) determines the width of the over all prior distribution of the effect.

a) y_k ~ x *B_k + B_0

b) B_k ~ N(mu, sigma)

c) mu ~ N(mu_hat,sigma_hat)

2. Here the individual B_k's would be effects of each individual model, but they are multiplied with a completely pooled, shared parameter A which is the same parameter for all the different models. Thus the sigma will say how much the B_k's can vary from each other and then the A will determine the over all effect.

aa)  y_k ~ x *A*B_k + B_0

bb) B_k ~ N(mu, sigma)

cc) A ~ N(mu_hat, sigma_hat)

Now the equations are different, but the design of the models are supposed to work in the same way.
But do they? Can we implement some sort of a matt-trick for the second version? And btw I can see how correlations may be very troublesome between all the B_k's and the A in the second case.

Best regards,
Jökull Snæbjarnarson

For my original problem here, I want to note that I also had made a dumb mistake before in simulating the data, which was to take in the mean output instead of a single draw -- I thought I was simulating a single draw from a single chain, in which case the mean IS the single draw, but I forgot that stan has a default chains = 4. Having fixed those 2 issues, the model works pretty well although it still seems to do something weird with the Sigma that I think is related to the ordering I've imposed on the vectors.

Basically, if I say ordered_draw ~ multi_normal(ordered_mean, Sigma) for some known ordered_mean and Sigma, that Sigma does not map exactly to the true_Sigma from which the draw is being drawn because the ordering creates additional positive covariance between draws for the reasons I outlined in an earlier post. But moreover, I now realise that (holding all else equal) having a higher variance in slot Sigma[i,i] means that the covariance between Sigma[i,i+1] is pushed up too since when extreme draws realise in slot [i], extreme draws have to realise in slot [i+1] to keep the ordering. This seems like an inherent property of drawing an ordered vector object and not a problem. Happy to hear opinions to the contrary, however.

messages.subject_clean: Strange/wrong results from using "ordered" type and "vector" type in same model?
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I think I may have discovered some issues with the interplay between objects of type "ordered" and objects of type "vector" in stan. To show these issues, let's consider a simplified version of a problem I'm working on. Let's say we are trying to simulate data from an ordered hierarchical multivariate normal model. The model is:

for( k in 1:K){
y[k] ~ multi_normal(beta_0_k[k], Sigma)
beta_0_k[k] ~ multi_normal(beta_0, Sigma)
}

I feed the model deterministic values for beta_0 and Sigma, I draw the beta_0_ks and the ys. The beta_0 and beta_0_k objects are of type "ordered". However, in the example I had in mind, the y might or might not be ordered (ie I might allow noise to mess up the ordering at that level of the model.) Now if the y is declared to be of type "ordered" the model gives the output it should logically give. But if y is declared to be type "vector" suddenly the model gives completely crazy results for the y draws, almost as if I were drawing from a standard normal no matter how big I make Sigma or how far from zero I make beta_0.

Attached is the simulation in R with the 2 stan models and the output in a .txt file.

Can someone familiar with the object types let us know why this is happening, and is there any way to allow y to be a vector type if beta_0_k is an ordered type?

Thank you all so much for your time and effort! I really appreciate it.

Cheers
Rachael

messages.body_plain:
The types are very simple.

  ordered[K] alpha;

means that alpha is constrained so that alpha[1] < alpha[2] < ... < alpha[K].
The actual transforms are in the chapter of the manual on transforms.  So
you get the Jacobian included in the log density.  alpha[1] = alpha_raw[1],
alpha[2] = alpha[1] + exp(alpha_raw[2], ...

But

  vector[K] y;

is just unconstrained.  So you shouldn't expect the results to
be ordered, even if you draw y from a multivariate normal with
ordered mean --- it'll come down to the covariance.  Do some
simulations outside of Stan and you'll see how it works.

- Bob

Thanks Bob! I think we are getting somewhere now. I agree maybe my intuition about them being "close" is off, but the output of the second model I showed is "off" enough that you can't then recover the parameters of the DGP if you fit the same model back to it for inference.

In the case you showed, at least the 2 vectors have roughly the same order of magnitude and the SEs are roughly similar. In the case I showed above, the unordered vector "y" output is on the wrong scale entirely (except in the first few slots of each vector). It's different from the underlying mean, beta_k_0 by more than an order of magnitude. This happens every time. Can that really be right? In this case y is not a good signal of its own mean! So we can't recover the beta_k_0 vector from seeing the y and that is seriously bad news for inference. :(

Maybe it helps to mention that if I then fit the same stan model to the output of the simulation with y declared as a vector, it never recovers the right parameters -- the inference model thinks the y's are drawn from a multivariate standard normal with correlation 1 across slots, when in reality y's are drawn from the beta_0_ks shown in the simulation and the Sigma matrix as defined in the R code I posted above. This is even when the variable types are kept consistent across the simulation model and the inference model. This is the real problem I'm trying to solve: I might get a non-ordered y due to a noisy estimation procedure or noise in the draw, but i know that there is a logical constraint on the beta_k_0 (ie the mean of y's sampling distribution) so that it must be ordered. I want to estimate that beta_k_0 from the y, imposing that it be ordered, even when I see non-ordered y.

Perhaps this very unhappy result is occuring because the Sigma in my simulation has a positive correlation across the slots, so that the first "y" draw then traps the rest of the y vector down there? I guess that could be the problem, but the variation allowed by the Sigma is so much larger than what I see with the y output that it doesn't seem able to explain all of the result.
