messages.body_plain:
I have been re-working in WinBUGS a Hidden Markov Model that was initially written by Simon Jackman to pool the polls over an election campaign <http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10361140500302472>. I have included the original article, replication package, and a recent update by Professor Jackman. I also have included my R code, WinBUGS code and data. I have been prompted to increase my computational efficiency because running the model takes quite a while. I have only this last week downloaded RStan, then went hunting for a HMM example so I could learn from example. I came across a lot more complex examples that I anticipated, for example <https://github.com/jrnold/ssmodels-in-stan/blob/master/stan-functions/dlm.stan>, and I am struggling to interpret the Stan language despite reading the Stan reference manual. I do not have a statistical or computational background and I am intending to learn Stan as I do my PhD. As there is an election campaign in Australia where I live and I research Australian elections, I've found a sudden need to improve my computational efficiency.

I was hoping someone could explain how to translate the BUGS model below into Stan.

Please have some patience and many thanks in advance.

model{
 ## measurement model
 for(i in 1:NPOLLS){
       mu[i] <- house[org[i]] + alpha[date[i]]
       y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i],prec[i])
 }

 ## transition model (aka random walk prior)
 for(i in 2:NPERIODS){
        mu.alpha[i] <- alpha[i-1]
        alpha[i] ~ dnorm(mu.alpha[i],tau)
 }

 ## priors
 tau <- 1/pow(sigma,2)   ## deterministic transform to precision
 sigma ~ dunif(0,.01)    ## uniform prior on standard deviation

 alpha[1] ~ dunif(.4,.6) ## initialization of daily track

 for(i in 1:13){          ## vague normal priors for house effects
       house[i] ~ dnorm(0,.01)
 }

}

The R code I'm using to set up my WinBUGS code is below.
data <- read.csv("8 may polls.csv",header=TRUE)
data$date.j <- julian(as.Date(as.vector(data$date),"%d-%m-%y"),origin=as.Date("1996-03-02"))
data$date.st <http://date.st> <- as.numeric(data$date.j)

## convert result and sample size to variance
data$y <- data$LNP2PP/100
data$var <- data$y*(1-data$y)/data$sample

## compute upper and lower bounds
data$sd <- sqrt(data$var)
data$lo <- data$y - 1.96*data$sd
data$up <- data$y + 1.96*data$sd

data$org <- as.integer(data$pollster)

## Date to predict to

predend <- 1 + julian(as.Date("2016-05-26"),format="%Y-%m-%d", origin=as.Date("1996-03-02"))

## set up WinBUGS

library(R2WinBUGS)

## set up data lists

foo <- list()

foo$y <- data$LNP2PP/100 # set recale percentage to 0 to 1
var <- foo$y*(1-foo$y)/data$sample # calculate variance
foo$prec <- 1/var
foo$date <- as.numeric(data$date.j)  ## set 2 March 1996, election day, as 1
foo$org <- data$org ## there are 13 in the data set
foo$NPOLLS <- length(data$y) ## there are 2001 polls
foo$alpha <- c(.5363,rep(NA,length(2:945)), ## there are 7 election results; Coalition 2PP
               .4902,rep(NA,length(947:2079)),
               .5095,rep(NA,length(2081:3143)),
               .5274,rep(NA,length(3145:4284)),
               .4730,rep(NA,length(4286:5285)),
               .4988,rep(NA,length(5287:6398)),
               .5349,rep(NA,length(6400:predend))) ## 26 May 2016 is day 7391
foo$NPERIODS <- length(foo$alpha)

## initial values for priors

initfunc <- function(){
  house <- rnorm(n=13,sd=.05)
  NPERIODS <- length(1:(max(foo$date)))
  alpha <- c(runif(n=7,.4,.6),  ## 7 election results
             runif(n=NPERIODS-7), ## length minus 7 election results
             NA) ## missing chain point
  sigma <- runif(n=1,0,.01)  ## uniform prior on standard deviation
  list(house=house, ## parameter - house effect
       alpha=alpha, ## parameter - chain
       sigma=sigma) ## standard deviation
}

## send to WinBUGS

daily <- bugs(data=foo,
              inits=initfunc,
              debug=TRUE,
              n.burnin=15000,
              n.iter=70000,
              n.thin=100,
              codaPkg=TRUE,
              parameters.to.save=c("alpha","house","sigma"),
              model.file="kalman bug 13.txt",bugs.directory="c:/WinBUGS14",
              program=c("winbugs"),useWINE=FALSE)

######## MUST MANUALLY CLOSE WinBUGS #####

## times for readings BUGS output

periodend <- length(foo$alpha)-7
housestart <- length(foo$alpha)-6
houseend <- length(foo$alpha)+6
sigmaend <- length(foo$alpha)+7

## read BUGS output back into R
library(coda)
alpha <- read.bugs(daily)
house <- alpha[,housestart:houseend]
sigma <- alpha[,sigmaend]
alpha <- alpha[,1:periodend]

alpha.bar <- apply(as.matrix(alpha),2,mean)
alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci> <- apply(as.matrix(alpha),2,quantile,c(.025,.975))

## estimates

alpha.bar <- c(.5363,as.matrix(alpha.bar)[1:944],.4902,as.matrix(alpha.bar)[945:2077],.5095,as.matrix(alpha.bar)[2078:3140],.5274,as.matrix(alpha.bar)[3141:4280],.4730,as.matrix(alpha.bar)[4281:5280],.4988,as.matrix(alpha.bar)[5281:6392],.5349,as.matrix(alpha.bar)[6393:length(alpha.bar)])
alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci> <- t(matrix(c(.5363,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[1,1:944],.4902,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[1,945:2077],.5095,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[1,2078:3140],.5274,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[1,3141:4280],.4730,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[1,4281:5280],.4988,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[1,5281:6392],.5349,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[1,6393:length(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)],
                       .5363,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[2,1:944],.4902,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[2,945:2077],.5095,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[2,2078:3140],.5274,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[2,3141:4280],.4730,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[2,4281:5280],.4988,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[2,5281:6392],.5349,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[2,6393:length(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)]),nrow=length(alpha.bar),ncol=2))

### estimate on final day of chain
alpha.bar[length(alpha.bar)]
### lower credibility interval
alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>[1,length(alpha.bar)]
### upper credibility interval
alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>[2,length(alpha.bar)]

         #####

houseEffects <- round(apply(as.matrix(house),2,function(x)c(mean(x),quantile(x,c(.025,.975))))*100,1)
dimnames(houseEffects)[[2]] <- levels(data$pollster)

         ## summary statistics for average
houseSum <- apply(as.matrix(house),1,mean)
mean(houseSum)*100
quantile(houseSum,c(.025,.975))*100
write.csv(houseEffects,file = "In-houseeffectsMansillo26mayl2016.csv")

         #### save daily estimates

dest <- cbind(alpha.bar,alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>[1,],alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>[2,])
colnames(dest)[1]<-"alpha.bar.mean"
colnames(dest)[2:3]<-c("alpha.bar.low.95","alpha.bar.upper.95")
write.csv(dest,file = "Coalition2PP2March1996Mansillo26may2016.csv")

There's an HMM example in the manual, but that involves
discrete state spaces that get marginalized out.
Your model has only continuous parameters (I think --- the
BUGS/JAGS models don't declare variable types), so you
don't need to do that (though in some cases, if everything's
conjugate, you can marginalize out the continuous states,
as in Kalman filters).

We don't recommend interval priors like this, and they
behave very differently in BUGS/JAGS than Stan for scale
parameters, because they use 1 / sigma^2 parameterizations.

>  sigma ~ dunif(0,.01)    ## uniform prior on standard deviation

are almost certainly bad news.  It means your parameter with
scale sigma is going to have small variation.  We recommend (see
the manual chapter on regression and Wiki page on prior
recommendations) unbounded <lower=0> constrained parameters for
scales with weakly informative priors.

Same here, only with no lower or upper-bound constraints.

>  alpha[1] ~ dunif(.4,.6) ## initialization of daily track

- Bob

you're worried about.  You can just put a prior on the centered
vector components directly.  The transform is linear, so there's
no Jacobian needed.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Should the sum-to-zero constrain added before sampling or after sampling?

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,
I think it's better to clarify my problem in code. I just wrote a scratch and there may some mistakes, but I just want to show the idea in my mind and I'm testing and modifying my code.

The whole idea about my model is jointly model two spatial variable, by explicitly define their cross covariance matrix (Not the precision, that's why the inverse can not be avoided). Suppose I have two spatial variables, y1 and y2, and let Y = c(y1, y2). Y is modeled by a Poisson regression framework, and using the log link, the
log_p = alpha + u + error;
for each variable, there will be a different alpha
u is the spatial effect for y1 and y2, follows a MVN(0, Sigma), where Sigma is a matrix of 4 blocks. The diagonal blocks are the usual covariance matrix for spatial CAR models, and the off-diagonal blocks are the matrix telling how the two spatial variables are correlated across maps.

In order to identify alpha and u, I need to center u. That's why I followed Kyle Foreman's code.
Here is the scratch of the code:
data{
  int<lower=0> J1;#number of spatial regions for map 1
  int<lower=0> J2;#number of spatial regions for map 2
  int Y[J1+J2];#event counts for two maps, modeled in Poisson regression
  int pop[J1+J2];#corresponding population, offset
  matrix[J1, J1] W_1; #adgacency matrix for the first map
  matrix[J2, J2] W_2; #adgacency matrix for the first map
  matrix[J1, J1] D_1; #diagonal matrix with diag elemetns being number of neighbors
  matrix[J2, J2] D_2; #diagonal matrix with diag elemetns being number of neighbors
  matrix[J1, J2] Psi_12# a matrix to indicate how the regions in 2 maps are correlated
}
transformed data {
  # zeros for MVN prior
  vector[N] zeros;
  zeros <- rep_vector(0.0, N);
}
parameters{
  real<lower=0, upper=1> rho[2]; #strength of spatial correlation, for two maps
  vector[J1+J2] u; #spatial effect for two maps
  real<lower=-0.3,upper=0.3> gamma12;#correlation between two maps, restriced for positive definiteness
  vector[2] alpha; #intercept for each spatial map
  vector[J1+J2] epsilon;# standard Normal
  real<lower=0> sigma2; #variance for the error term in log mean of Poisson
  vector[2] delta;#variance compentent of the CAR model
}
transformed parameters{
  real<lower=0> sigma; #sqrt of sigma2
  sigma  <-  sqrt(sigma2);
}
model{
   matrix[J1, J1] B_1; #precision matrix for the 1st map
   matrix[J2, J2] B_2; #precision matrix for the 1st map
   matrix[J1+J2, J1+J2] Sigma;#covariance matrix for spatial effect;
   matrix[J1+J2, J1+J2] Sigma_full;#covariance matrix for spatial effect;
   vector[J1+J2] epsilon;# parameter for Poisson distribution in log scale
   vector[J1+J2] alpha_vec;#broadcast the intercept
   vector[J1+J2] delta_vec;#broadcast the variance compentent
   matrix[J1+J2, J1+J2] DELTA;#cange delta_vec to diag matrix

   delta_vec[1:J1] <- rep_vector(delta[1], J1);
   delta_vec[(J1+1):J2] <- rep_vector(delta[2], J2);
   DELTA <- diag_matrix(delta_vec)
   alpha_vec[1:J1] <- rep_vector(alpha[1], J1);
   alpha_vec[(J1+1):J2] <- rep_vector(alpha[2], J2);
   B_1 <- D_1 - rho[1] * W_1;
   B_2 <- D_2 - rho[2] * W_2;
   #assign Sigma in block
   #Sigma = DELTA%*%
     #B_1_inv             gamma12*Psi_12
     #t(gamma12*Psi_12)   B_2_inv
   #%*%DELTA
   Sigma[1:J1, 1:J1] <- inverse_spd(B_1);
   Sigma[(J1+1):(J1+J2), (J1+1):(J1+J2)] <- inverse_spd(B_2);
   Sigma[1:J1, (J1+J2)] <- gamma12 * Psi_12;
   Sigma[(J1+1), 1:J1] <- (Sigma[1:J1, (J1+J2)])';
   Sigma_full <- DELTA*Sigma*DELTA;
   #prior for the spatial effect
   u ~ multi_normal(zeros, Sigma_full);
   epsilon ~ normal(0,1);
   log_p <- log(pop) + alpha_vec + u + sigma*epsilon;
   y ~ poisson_log(log_p);#likelihood
}

And based on your suggestions, is this the correct way doing the centering?
parameters{
  simplex[J1+J2] z;#std normal
}

model{
  matrix[J1+J2, J1+J2] L;#cholesky of SIgma_full
  z ~ normal(0,1);
  L <- cholesky_decompose(Sigma_full);
  u <- L*z;
}

Thanks. Jiang

Hi Mahdi, do you mean how do you get quantiles other than the defaults of 2.5%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 97.5%? If you're using RStan and you want the 12% quantile for each parameter then you can do

fit_summary <- summary(fit, probs = c(0.12))
fit_summary$summary[, "12%"]

The object fit_summary will be a list with two components, c_summary and summary, the former giving you the summary for each chain, and the latter with all chains combined.

Hope that helps,

Jonah

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Two ways of hierarchical pooling (warning it's more of a math discussion, than stan)
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Two ways of hierarchical pooling (warning it's more of a math discussion, than stan)
messages.body_plain:
In the future be careful with hats — in statistics they are usually
reserved for estimators which are functions of the data and not
hyperparameters.  For example, less than careful reading of this
post by a statistician could easily be confused for something like
an empirical Bayes approximation where you plug in data estimates
for hyperpriors.

Notation aside, (1) and (2) are not equivalent.  Firstly, mu and sigma
always need priors, so even if you introduce A in (2) then you still
need to define a prior for mu or you haven’t fully specified your model.

More importantly, mu has the effect of translating the B_k, not scaling
them.  This is easier to see if you write (1) with a non-centered parameterization,

y_{k} ~ N( x * (mu + sigma * B_k) + B_{0}, upsilon)
B_k ~ N(0, 1)
// hyperpriors for mu, sigma, and upsilon

mu just shifts the overall effect, while sigma is responsible for scaling
the individual effects.  So if you introduced an A that multiplies x then
you would be affecting the variance of the population.

If you’re careful then you could manipulate this into an equivalent model,
but then you’d have a non-identifiability between A and sigma.  In other
words, you’re just replacing alpha by (alpha_{1} + alpha_{2}) which is
technically valid but will make the model much harder to fit for no good
reason.

On May 24, 2016, at 3:15 PM, Jökull Snæbjarnarson <jok...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hey guys,
> Sorry if this doesn't belong on this mailing list. I just couldn't find a better place to ask the question
>
> I'm wondering if anyone of you could tell me any real difference and/or advantage to the following two methods of partial pooling in those simple regression models.
>
> 1. example.
> For each response variable y_k, (where k = (1:N), each k could e.g. be a different school or country), we want to model the effect of data x on the data y_k, by sampling B_k and an intercept B_0. Assuming all y's are related we pool the B_k towards each other by sampling the mean of each B_k from the same hyper prior. Thus the sigma in b) says how much each B_k are allowed to vary from each other but the sigma_hat in c) determines the width of the over all prior distribution of the effect.
>
> a) y_k ~ x *B_k + B_0
>
> b) B_k ~ N(mu, sigma)
>
> c) mu ~ N(mu_hat,sigma_hat)
>
>
> 2. Here the individual B_k's would be effects of each individual model, but they are multiplied with a completely pooled, shared parameter A which is the same parameter for all the different models. Thus the sigma will say how much the B_k's can vary from each other and then the A will determine the over all effect.
>
> aa)  y_k ~ x *A*B_k + B_0
>
> bb) B_k ~ N(mu, sigma)
>
> cc) A ~ N(mu_hat, sigma_hat)
>
>
> Now the equations are different, but the design of the models are supposed to work in the same way.
> But do they? Can we implement some sort of a matt-trick for the second version? And btw I can see how correlations may be very troublesome between all the B_k's and the A in the second case.
>
> Best regards,
> Jökull Snæbjarnarson
>
>
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Two ways of hierarchical pooling (warning it's more of a math discussion, than stan)
messages.body_plain:
The whole point of a hierarchical model is to let
sigma (and mu) be a parameter and learn it from
the population data!  Uniform priors, however, put
way too much probability at high values of B/sigma
where there is no pooling of the B at all.

On May 26, 2016, at 1:39 PM, Jökull Snæbjarnarson <jok...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks for the reply, I'll try to be more careful with the hats :)
>
> And ok yes I get the non-identifiability.
>

> But I think i'm lacking some understanding of the need for a prior of the sigma. Could you explain or point me towards some literature?
> Is there difference of the distribution of B in this case:
>
> y ~ x*B+B0
> B ~ uniform[0,inf]
>
> and
>
> y ~ x*B+B0
> B~ N(0,sigma)
> sigma ~ uniform[0,inf]
>
> -Jökull
>

>
> On Thursday, May 26, 2016 at 11:41:25 AM UTC+2, Michael Betancourt wrote:

> > In the future be careful with hats — in statistics they are usually
> > reserved for estimators which are functions of the data and not
> > hyperparameters.  For example, less than careful reading of this
> > post by a statistician could easily be confused for something like
> > an empirical Bayes approximation where you plug in data estimates
> > for hyperpriors.
> >
> > Notation aside, (1) and (2) are not equivalent.  Firstly, mu and sigma
> > always need priors, so even if you introduce A in (2) then you still
> > need to define a prior for mu or you haven’t fully specified your model.
> >
> > More importantly, mu has the effect of translating the B_k, not scaling
> > them.  This is easier to see if you write (1) with a non-centered parameterization,
> >
> > y_{k} ~ N( x * (mu + sigma * B_k) + B_{0}, upsilon)
> > B_k ~ N(0, 1)
> > // hyperpriors for mu, sigma, and upsilon
> >
> > mu just shifts the overall effect, while sigma is responsible for scaling
> > the individual effects.  So if you introduced an A that multiplies x then
> > you would be affecting the variance of the population.
> >
> > If you’re careful then you could manipulate this into an equivalent model,
> > but then you’d have a non-identifiability between A and sigma.  In other
> > words, you’re just replacing alpha by (alpha_{1} + alpha_{2}) which is
> > technically valid but will make the model much harder to fit for no good
> > reason.
> >
> > On May 24, 2016, at 3:15 PM, Jökull Snæbjarnarson <jok...@gmail.com <http://gmail.com/>> wrote:
> >
> > > Hey guys,
> > > Sorry if this doesn't belong on this mailing list. I just couldn't find a better place to ask the question
> > >
> > > I'm wondering if anyone of you could tell me any real difference and/or advantage to the following two methods of partial pooling in those simple regression models.
> > >
> > > 1. example.
> > > For each response variable y_k, (where k = (1:N), each k could e.g. be a different school or country), we want to model the effect of data x on the data y_k, by sampling B_k and an intercept B_0. Assuming all y's are related we pool the B_k towards each other by sampling the mean of each B_k from the same hyper prior. Thus the sigma in b) says how much each B_k are allowed to vary from each other but the sigma_hat in c) determines the width of the over all prior distribution of the effect.
> > >
> > > a) y_k ~ x *B_k + B_0
> > >
> > > b) B_k ~ N(mu, sigma)
> > >
> > > c) mu ~ N(mu_hat,sigma_hat)
> > >
> > >
> > > 2. Here the individual B_k's would be effects of each individual model, but they are multiplied with a completely pooled, shared parameter A which is the same parameter for all the different models. Thus the sigma will say how much the B_k's can vary from each other and then the A will determine the over all effect.
> > >
> > > aa)  y_k ~ x *A*B_k + B_0

> > > bb) B_k ~ N(mu, sigma)

> > > Now the equations are different, but the design of the models are supposed to work in the same way.
> > > But do they? Can we implement some sort of a matt-trick for the second version? And btw I can see how correlations may be very troublesome between all the B_k's and the A in the second case.

Unfortunately there is little literature on the estimation of quantiles
from samples, but you see some of the issues in Andy’s paper,
http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/HPD_STCO.pdf.

The biggest challenge with these quantile estimators is that it’s
hard to assign confidence intervals because they’re not quite
expectations and hence don’t quite fall into MCMC central
limit theorems.  But if you don’t believe me then simulate it
yourself — start with IID gaussian draws and see how many
samples it takes to accurate pin down the extreme quantiles.

messages.subject_clean: Slow sampling of educational measurement model (hierarchical logistic regression model)
messages.body_plain:
I can't precisely explain why, but it appears that using a bernoulii prior with the predictors specified as as 1 / (1-exp(x))  rather than a bernoulli_logit is a significant performance boost. JAGS displays similar behavior, so the bernoulli_logit transformation of the predictors must have an impact on the log density that makes it much more time consuming to sample from.

Anyone have any other ideas?

On Friday, May 20, 2016 at 2:30:50 PM UTC-6, David Rackham wrote:
> Hi everyone,
>
> I am trying to implement a hierarchical logistic regression model that is somewhat related to the IRT class of models but has a few differences. For context, I am using simulated data to assess the performance of my implementation of the Reduced-DINA model (a type of Educational measurement model).
>
> The data are student's responses (1 = correct, 0 = incorrect) to a 30 item test that measures two latent attributes (or skills). Items 1-10 measure skill1, items 11-20 measure skill2, and items 21-30 measure skills 1 and 2. (Note: this relationship is established in a Q-matrix, but does not appear in my implementation of the model). The likelihood for an item that measures both skills (alpha1 and alpha2) is:
>
> logit p(Y[student, item] | alpha[1], alpha[2]) = f[item] + d[item] * alpha[1] * alpha[2]
>
> The likelihood for an item that measures only skill 1 (alpha1) is:
>
> logit p(Y[student, item] | alpha[1]) = f[item] + d[item] * alpha[1]
>
> Essentially f[item] acts as the baseline probability of correctly answering the question if you have not mastered all of the required skills and d[item] is the additive increase in the probability of a correct response for mastering all required skills.  In my data simulation I am tightly controlling f and d to ensure that if the student has not mastered the skills the probability of a correct response is less than 5%. If the student has mastered the skills the probability of a correct response is greater than 95%.
>
> I've implemented the model in Stan as:
>
> data {
>   int<lower=1> I;           // number of examinees
>   int<lower=1> J;           // number of items
>   int<lower=1> K;           // number of skills
>   int<lower=0, upper=1> y[I,J];            // correctness of examinee on item
> }
>
> parameters {
>   real<lower=-20, upper=20> fHat[J];              // intercept or baseline probability
>   real<lower=-20, upper=20> dHat[J];              // main effect of skill mastery
>   real<lower=0, upper=1> alpha1[I];
>   real<lower=0, upper=1> alpha2[I];
>
>   real <lower=0, upper=50> a1[I];
>   real <lower=0, upper=50> b1[I];
>   real <lower=0, upper=50> a2[I];
>   real <lower=0, upper=50> b2[I];
> }
>
> model {
>   # priors for continous skill mastery
>   for (i in 1:I){
>     alpha1[i] ~ beta(a1[i],b1[i]);
>     alpha2[i] ~ beta(a2[i],b2[i]);
>   }
>
>   a1 ~ cauchy(0,5);
>   b1 ~ cauchy(0,5);
>
>   a2 ~ cauchy(0,5);
>   b2 ~ cauchy(0,5);
>
>   # priors for RDINA parameters d and f
>   dHat ~ normal(7,2);
>   fHat ~ normal(-3,2);
>
>
>   for (i in 1:I){
>     y[i,1] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[1] + (dHat[1] * alpha1[i]));
>     # items 2 - 9 omitted
>     y[i,10] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[10] + (dHat[10] * alpha1[i]));
>
>     y[i,11] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[11] + (dHat[11] * alpha2[i]));
>     # items 12 - 19 omitted
>     y[i,20] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[20] + (dHat[20] * alpha2[i]));
>
>     y[i,21] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[21] + (dHat[21] * alpha1[i] * alpha2[i]));
>     # items 22 - 29 omitted
>     y[i,30] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[30] + (dHat[30] * alpha1[i] * alpha2[i]));
>   }
> }
>
>
> Currently when I run the model using 1,000 students it takes about 18 hours to finish sampling (using 4 chains of n = 2000 on 4 cores). While this is obviously not terrible relative to some of the models I've read about on the list, I'd like to reduce the sampling time if at all possible as I will be conducting a large number of simulations using variations of this model.
>
> Here are things I've explored, but been unable to resolve:
> Fully vectorizing the response data such that y is a vector length # Items x # students (similar to the IRT model examples). The issue with this is I haven't been able to figure out how to selectively include alpha1 and alpha2 depending on whether or not the item measures those skills. My linear algebra skills are weak, so there may be an easy implementation that I am missing (perhaps a Kronecker delta function of some sort?).
> A non-hierarchical model samples much more quickly, but I am using the hierarchical priors on alpha1 and alpha2 to help push the parameter values to 0 or 1. In JAGS I used a binomial prior on alpha1 and alpha2 but obviously STAN does not support that.
> Would anyone be kind enough to point me in the direction of some optimizations? Or any suggestions of where to look? I am new to both STAN and this type of model, so I imagine I am overlooking many things.
>
> Many thanks in advance!
>
> -Dave
>
>

messages.body_plain:
That's a different link function.  inverse logit is 1 / (1 + exp(-x)) not
1 / (1 - exp(x)).  In your case, if x > log(1), you get a negative value.

We don't recommend constraining your parameters to intervals unless
necessary to satisfy physical constraints --- we recommend weakly informative
or even more strongly informative priors about the scale of the expected
answers instead.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I think you guys may be talking past each other.

I think Mahdi's asking for how you assign confidence
to a parameter estimate, not how you calculate confidence
intervals for MCMC estimators of quantiles (though I
am interested in hearing more about the answer to that
question given that they're not expectations).

Mahdi --- those posterior intervals are Bayesian and any text
on Bayes should explain what's going on.  They are not
highest posterior density intervals, just central ones.  And
by all means do what Michael suggests in terms of pinning down
extreme quantiles.  We should have that in a tutorial somewhere.

- Bob

> On May 26, 2016, at 10:37 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Unfortunately there is little literature on the estimation of quantiles
> from samples, but you see some of the issues in Andy’s paper,
> http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/HPD_STCO.pdf.
>
> The biggest challenge with these quantile estimators is that it’s
> hard to assign confidence intervals because they’re not quite
> expectations and hence don’t quite fall into MCMC central
> limit theorems.  But if you don’t believe me then simulate it
> yourself — start with IID gaussian draws and see how many
> samples it takes to accurate pin down the extreme quantiles.
>
> On May 26, 2016, at 3:24 PM, Mahdi Akbarzadeh <akbarz...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> Then what is the confidence coefficient for that? (5%-95%)?

>>
>>
>> On Thu, May 26, 2016 at 6:35 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> No, they are empirical percentiles estimated from the MCMC
>> draws.  In particular, the 2.5% and 97.5% estimates are very
>> very noisy and we do not recommend using then to estimate
>> a HPD interval.  A 5%-95% interval is relatively robust but a
>> 10%-90% is even better while still giving you a good idea of
>> the posterior concentration.
>>
>> On May 26, 2016, at 2:28 PM, Mahdi Akbarzadeh <akbarz...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>>> These values are percentiles of the parameter posterior distribution. I use them as HPD intervals (0.025 and 0.0975).
>>>
>>> On Thu, May 26, 2016 at 2:43 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>> Note that these yield MCMC _estimates_ of the posterior quantiles,
>>> not exact values.  In particular, quantiles below 5% and above 95%
>>> are notoriously hard to estimate and the estimators will be really
>>> noisy.
>>>
>>> On May 25, 2016, at 3:41 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow sampling of educational measurement model (hierarchical logistic regression model)
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Slow sampling of educational measurement model (hierarchical logistic regression model)
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Bob! It looks like my response was a typo, rather than an error in my implementation. I implemented it as:

y[i, 1] ~ bernoulli(1 / (1 + exp(-fHat[1] - dHat[1] * (alpha1[i] * alpha2[i]))));

What suggestions do you have for the priors? And are you referring specifically to the dHat and fHat normal priors? And to be clear, Stan does not require interval constraints on reals?

Thanks!

> On May 26, 2016, at 1:01 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>

> That's a different link function.  inverse logit is 1 / (1 + exp(-x)) not
> 1 / (1 - exp(x)).  In your case, if x > log(1), you get a negative value.
>
> We don't recommend constraining your parameters to intervals unless
> necessary to satisfy physical constraints --- we recommend weakly informative
> or even more strongly informative priors about the scale of the expected
> answers instead.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On May 26, 2016, at 12:13 PM, David Rackham <ddra...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > I can't precisely explain why, but it appears that using a bernoulii prior with the predictors specified as as 1 / (1-exp(x))  rather than a bernoulli_logit is a significant performance boost. JAGS displays similar behavior, so the bernoulli_logit transformation of the predictors must have an impact on the log density that makes it much more time consuming to sample from.
> >
> > Anyone have any other ideas?
> >
> > On Friday, May 20, 2016 at 2:30:50 PM UTC-6, David Rackham wrote:
> > Hi everyone,
> >
> > I am trying to implement a hierarchical logistic regression model that is somewhat related to the IRT class of models but has a few differences. For context, I am using simulated data to assess the performance of my implementation of the Reduced-DINA model (a type of Educational measurement model).
> >
> > The data are student's responses (1 = correct, 0 = incorrect) to a 30 item test that measures two latent attributes (or skills). Items 1-10 measure skill1, items 11-20 measure skill2, and items 21-30 measure skills 1 and 2. (Note: this relationship is established in a Q-matrix, but does not appear in my implementation of the model). The likelihood for an item that measures both skills (alpha1 and alpha2) is:
> >
> > logit p(Y[student, item] | alpha[1], alpha[2]) = f[item] + d[item] * alpha[1] * alpha[2]
> >
> > The likelihood for an item that measures only skill 1 (alpha1) is:
> >
> > logit p(Y[student, item] | alpha[1]) = f[item] + d[item] * alpha[1]
> >
> > Essentially f[item] acts as the baseline probability of correctly answering the question if you have not mastered all of the required skills and d[item] is the additive increase in the probability of a correct response for mastering all required skills.  In my data simulation I am tightly controlling f and d to ensure that if the student has not mastered the skills the probability of a correct response is less than 5%. If the student has mastered the skills the probability of a correct response is greater than 95%.
> >
> > I've implemented the model in Stan as:
> >
> > data {
> >  int<lower=1> I;           // number of examinees
> >  int<lower=1> J;           // number of items
> >  int<lower=1> K;           // number of skills
> >  int<lower=0, upper=1> y[I,J];            // correctness of examinee on item
> > }
> >
> > parameters {
> >  real<lower=-20, upper=20> fHat[J];              // intercept or baseline probability
> >  real<lower=-20, upper=20> dHat[J];              // main effect of skill mastery
> >  real<lower=0, upper=1> alpha1[I];
> >  real<lower=0, upper=1> alpha2[I];
> >
> >  real <lower=0, upper=50> a1[I];
> >  real <lower=0, upper=50> b1[I];
> >  real <lower=0, upper=50> a2[I];
> >  real <lower=0, upper=50> b2[I];
> > }
> >
> > model {
> >  # priors for continous skill mastery
> >  for (i in 1:I){
> >    alpha1[i] ~ beta(a1[i],b1[i]);
> >    alpha2[i] ~ beta(a2[i],b2[i]);
> >  }
> >
> >  a1 ~ cauchy(0,5);
> >  b1 ~ cauchy(0,5);
> >
> >  a2 ~ cauchy(0,5);
> >  b2 ~ cauchy(0,5);
> >
> >  # priors for RDINA parameters d and f
> >  dHat ~ normal(7,2);
> >  fHat ~ normal(-3,2);
> >
> >
> >  for (i in 1:I){
> >    y[i,1] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[1] + (dHat[1] * alpha1[i]));
> >    # items 2 - 9 omitted
> >    y[i,10] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[10] + (dHat[10] * alpha1[i]));
> >
> >    y[i,11] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[11] + (dHat[11] * alpha2[i]));
> >    # items 12 - 19 omitted
> >    y[i,20] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[20] + (dHat[20] * alpha2[i]));
> >
> >    y[i,21] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[21] + (dHat[21] * alpha1[i] * alpha2[i]));
> >    # items 22 - 29 omitted
> >    y[i,30] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[30] + (dHat[30] * alpha1[i] * alpha2[i]));
> >  }
> > }
> >
> >
> > Currently when I run the model using 1,000 students it takes about 18 hours to finish sampling (using 4 chains of n = 2000 on 4 cores). While this is obviously not terrible relative to some of the models I've read about on the list, I'd like to reduce the sampling time if at all possible as I will be conducting a large number of simulations using variations of this model.
> >
> > Here are things I've explored, but been unable to resolve:
> > • Fully vectorizing the response data such that y is a vector length # Items x # students (similar to the IRT model examples). The issue with this is I haven't been able to figure out how to selectively include alpha1 and alpha2 depending on whether or not the item measures those skills. My linear algebra skills are weak, so there may be an easy implementation that I am missing (perhaps a Kronecker delta function of some sort?).
> > • A non-hierarchical model samples much more quickly, but I am using the hierarchical priors on alpha1 and alpha2 to help push the parameter values to 0 or 1. In JAGS I used a binomial prior on alpha1 and alpha2 but obviously STAN does not support that.
> > Would anyone be kind enough to point me in the direction of some optimizations? Or any suggestions of where to look? I am new to both STAN and this type of model, so I imagine I am overlooking many things.
> >
> > Many thanks in advance!
> >
> > -Dave
> >
> >
> > I doubt it will be helpful, but here is the sessionInfo information as requested:
> > R version 3.2.5 (2016-04-14)
> > Platform: x86_64-pc-linux-gnu (64-bit)

messages.body_plain:
That shouldn't be faster than

  y[i, 1] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[1] + dHat[1] * (alpha1[i] * alpha2[i]));

Try more runs and see if your first impressions hold up.

Also, we have an inv_logit() function specifically so users don't
have to reimplement things like this themselves.

Any time you have alpha1[i] * alpha2[i] like this it's going
to be a problem (assuming alpha1 and alpha2 are parameters).  It's
not identified by itself and causes a banana-shaped posterior that's
hard to sample.

- Bob

> On May 26, 2016, at 4:15 PM, David Rackham <ddra...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks Bob! It looks like my response was a typo, rather than an error in my implementation. I implemented it as:
>
> y[i, 1] ~ bernoulli(1 / (1 + exp(-fHat[1] - dHat[1] * (alpha1[i] * alpha2[i]))));
>
> What suggestions do you have for the priors? And are you referring specifically to the dHat and fHat normal priors? And to be clear, Stan does not require interval constraints on reals?
>
> Thanks!
>
>> On May 26, 2016, at 1:01 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>
>> That's a different link function.  inverse logit is 1 / (1 + exp(-x)) not
>> 1 / (1 - exp(x)).  In your case, if x > log(1), you get a negative value.
>>
>> We don't recommend constraining your parameters to intervals unless
>> necessary to satisfy physical constraints --- we recommend weakly informative
>> or even more strongly informative priors about the scale of the expected
>> answers instead.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>> On May 26, 2016, at 12:13 PM, David Rackham <ddra...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> I can't precisely explain why, but it appears that using a bernoulii prior with the predictors specified as as 1 / (1-exp(x))  rather than a bernoulli_logit is a significant performance boost. JAGS displays similar behavior, so the bernoulli_logit transformation of the predictors must have an impact on the log density that makes it much more time consuming to sample from.
>>>
>>> Anyone have any other ideas?
>>>
>>> On Friday, May 20, 2016 at 2:30:50 PM UTC-6, David Rackham wrote:
>>> Hi everyone,
>>>
>>> I am trying to implement a hierarchical logistic regression model that is somewhat related to the IRT class of models but has a few differences. For context, I am using simulated data to assess the performance of my implementation of the Reduced-DINA model (a type of Educational measurement model).
>>>
>>> The data are student's responses (1 = correct, 0 = incorrect) to a 30 item test that measures two latent attributes (or skills). Items 1-10 measure skill1, items 11-20 measure skill2, and items 21-30 measure skills 1 and 2. (Note: this relationship is established in a Q-matrix, but does not appear in my implementation of the model). The likelihood for an item that measures both skills (alpha1 and alpha2) is:
>>>
>>> logit p(Y[student, item] | alpha[1], alpha[2]) = f[item] + d[item] * alpha[1] * alpha[2]
>>>
>>> The likelihood for an item that measures only skill 1 (alpha1) is:
>>>
>>> logit p(Y[student, item] | alpha[1]) = f[item] + d[item] * alpha[1]
>>>
>>> Essentially f[item] acts as the baseline probability of correctly answering the question if you have not mastered all of the required skills and d[item] is the additive increase in the probability of a correct response for mastering all required skills.  In my data simulation I am tightly controlling f and d to ensure that if the student has not mastered the skills the probability of a correct response is less than 5%. If the student has mastered the skills the probability of a correct response is greater than 95%.
>>>
>>> I've implemented the model in Stan as:
>>>
>>> data {
>>>  int<lower=1> I;           // number of examinees
>>>  int<lower=1> J;           // number of items
>>>  int<lower=1> K;           // number of skills
>>>  int<lower=0, upper=1> y[I,J];            // correctness of examinee on item
>>> }
>>>
>>> parameters {
>>>  real<lower=-20, upper=20> fHat[J];              // intercept or baseline probability
>>>  real<lower=-20, upper=20> dHat[J];              // main effect of skill mastery
>>>  real<lower=0, upper=1> alpha1[I];
>>>  real<lower=0, upper=1> alpha2[I];
>>>
>>>  real <lower=0, upper=50> a1[I];
>>>  real <lower=0, upper=50> b1[I];
>>>  real <lower=0, upper=50> a2[I];
>>>  real <lower=0, upper=50> b2[I];
>>> }
>>>
>>> model {
>>>  # priors for continous skill mastery
>>>  for (i in 1:I){
>>>    alpha1[i] ~ beta(a1[i],b1[i]);
>>>    alpha2[i] ~ beta(a2[i],b2[i]);
>>>  }
>>>
>>>  a1 ~ cauchy(0,5);
>>>  b1 ~ cauchy(0,5);
>>>
>>>  a2 ~ cauchy(0,5);
>>>  b2 ~ cauchy(0,5);
>>>
>>>  # priors for RDINA parameters d and f
>>>  dHat ~ normal(7,2);
>>>  fHat ~ normal(-3,2);
>>>
>>>
>>>  for (i in 1:I){
>>>    y[i,1] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[1] + (dHat[1] * alpha1[i]));
>>>    # items 2 - 9 omitted
>>>    y[i,10] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[10] + (dHat[10] * alpha1[i]));
>>>
>>>    y[i,11] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[11] + (dHat[11] * alpha2[i]));
>>>    # items 12 - 19 omitted
>>>    y[i,20] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[20] + (dHat[20] * alpha2[i]));
>>>
>>>    y[i,21] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[21] + (dHat[21] * alpha1[i] * alpha2[i]));
>>>    # items 22 - 29 omitted
>>>    y[i,30] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[30] + (dHat[30] * alpha1[i] * alpha2[i]));
>>>  }
>>> }
>>>
>>>
>>> Currently when I run the model using 1,000 students it takes about 18 hours to finish sampling (using 4 chains of n = 2000 on 4 cores). While this is obviously not terrible relative to some of the models I've read about on the list, I'd like to reduce the sampling time if at all possible as I will be conducting a large number of simulations using variations of this model.
>>>
>>> Here are things I've explored, but been unable to resolve:
>>> • Fully vectorizing the response data such that y is a vector length # Items x # students (similar to the IRT model examples). The issue with this is I haven't been able to figure out how to selectively include alpha1 and alpha2 depending on whether or not the item measures those skills. My linear algebra skills are weak, so there may be an easy implementation that I am missing (perhaps a Kronecker delta function of some sort?).
>>> • A non-hierarchical model samples much more quickly, but I am using the hierarchical priors on alpha1 and alpha2 to help push the parameter values to 0 or 1. In JAGS I used a binomial prior on alpha1 and alpha2 but obviously STAN does not support that.
>>> Would anyone be kind enough to point me in the direction of some optimizations? Or any suggestions of where to look? I am new to both STAN and this type of model, so I imagine I am overlooking many things.
>>>
>>> Many thanks in advance!
>>>
>>> -Dave

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for your advice. I've changed to use quad_form_diag when I was running the code.

The way I want to build a covariance requires to inverse some matrix, say B. I even tried using its cholesky part L (LL'=B), and then inverse L. I think stan doesn't have the particular inverse for triangular matrices. But still, the inverse matrix is really slow and it takes more than a hour for 100 iterations. So I give up some "interpretation ability" of my current covariance matrix and find a way doing on the precision matrix, and the model gave me reliable results (a hour with 5000 iterations and convergence met).

Here are some of my questions:
1. About the inverse. I did some Gibbs sampling involves the inverse of the covariance matrix as above in R, the speed is not that bad. Is that calculating the gradient making Stan not good at calculating the inverse? Since for a matrix not that huge (under 500*500), the inverse should be fast in C++ or R using the cholesky inverse method. (although  I  do try to avoid calculating the inverse every time when I'm programming, but this time the inverse is a must. )

2. When sampling from multivariate normal distribution, people usually use Cholesky decomposition to transfrom from a vector a N(0,1) random variables, which is fast. In stan, if u ~ multi_normal(0, Sigma), then which way is faster or better?
 One way is just specify as it is;
the other way is  u<-L*z where z~N(0,1), LL'=Sigma.
Or something like: u ~ multi_normal_cholesky(0, L) where LL'=Sigma.
And when using multi_normal(0, Sigma), will it be expensive since Stan will calculate the inverse under the hood? Or, how does stan calculate the log density of multi_normal when given a covariance matrix, not precision one.

Thanks,

Jiang

> > The whole idea about my model is jointly model two spatial variable, by explicitly define their cross covariance matrix (Not the precision, that's why the inverse can not be avoided). Suppose I have two spatial variables, y1 and y2, and let Y = c(y1, y2). Y is modeled by a Poisson regression framework, and using the log link, the
> > log_p = alpha + u + error;
> > for each variable, there will be a different alpha
> > u is the spatial effect for y1 and y2, follows a MVN(0, Sigma), where Sigma is a matrix of 4 blocks. The diagonal blocks are the usual covariance matrix for spatial CAR models, and the off-diagonal blocks are the matrix telling how the two spatial variables are correlated across maps.
> >
> > In order to identify alpha and u, I need to center u. That's why I followed Kyle Foreman's code.
> > Here is the scratch of the code:
> > data{
> >   int<lower=0> J1;#number of spatial regions for map 1
> >   int<lower=0> J2;#number of spatial regions for map 2

> >   matrix[J1, J1] W_1; #adgacency matrix for the first map
> >   matrix[J2, J2] W_2; #adgacency matrix for the first map
> >   matrix[J1, J1] D_1; #diagonal matrix with diag elemetns being number of neighbors
> >   matrix[J2, J2] D_2; #diagonal matrix with diag elemetns being number of neighbors

> > }
> > transformed data {

> >   vector[N] zeros;
> >   zeros <- rep_vector(0.0, N);
> > }
> > parameters{
> >   real<lower=0, upper=1> rho[2]; #strength of spatial correlation, for two maps
> >   vector[J1+J2] u; #spatial effect for two maps
> >   real<lower=-0.3,upper=0.3> gamma12;#correlation between two maps, restriced for positive definiteness
> >   vector[2] alpha; #intercept for each spatial map
> >   vector[J1+J2] epsilon;# standard Normal
> >   real<lower=0> sigma2; #variance for the error term in log mean of Poisson
> >   vector[2] delta;#variance compentent of the CAR model
> > }
> > transformed parameters{
> >   real<lower=0> sigma; #sqrt of sigma2
> >   sigma  <-  sqrt(sigma2);
> > }
> > model{
> >    matrix[J1, J1] B_1; #precision matrix for the 1st map
> >    matrix[J2, J2] B_2; #precision matrix for the 1st map
> >    matrix[J1+J2, J1+J2] Sigma;#covariance matrix for spatial effect;
> >    matrix[J1+J2, J1+J2] Sigma_full;#covariance matrix for spatial effect;
> >    vector[J1+J2] epsilon;# parameter for Poisson distribution in log scale
> >    vector[J1+J2] alpha_vec;#broadcast the intercept
> >    vector[J1+J2] delta_vec;#broadcast the variance compentent
> >    matrix[J1+J2, J1+J2] DELTA;#cange delta_vec to diag matrix

messages.body_plain:
I have a very large data set, which means I can only run one chain at a time without running out of RAM. I have access to a computing cluster, so I can run many Stan jobs in parallel on different machines, each running just one chain. Is there a best practice for bringing together these separate chains, so as to calculate Rhat (which I know is calculated across chains) and neff (which I'm not sure if it is).

I'm using Pystan, so more technically this question is really: Is there a way to combine multiple StanFit4model objects?

Thanks!
Jeff

messages.body_plain:
I am trying to fit a non-standard hierarchical model with the help of stan, but having some trouble. Basically, I would like to fit a hierarchical model similar to the 8 schools example from stan, except that rather than placing a hierarchical distribution on the random effects parameters, I want place the hierarchical distribution on the squared random effects parameters.

Why? You can think of the lower level parameters as a bunch of distances, measured for a bunch of different units. Within a unit, the sign on the distance has meaning (e.g., B-A > 0 implies B > A). But once we start averaging across units, the sign has no meaning, because for the first unit, I could calculate B-A or A-B, for the second unit, I could calculate C-D or D-C, etc. I want an estimate that looks at the overall magnitude of the errors, but doesn't depend on direction. Thus, the squaring. I thought if I put a Gamma distribution on the squared random effect parameters, then I could think of the estimated mean of the hierarchical distribution as the mean squared distance (or MSE). But after lots of tinkering with stan, I can't make it converge.

Here is my stan model (also attached):
data {
  int<lower=0> J; // number of units
  real d[J]; // estimated distances
  real<lower=0> sigma[J]; // s.e. of distance estimates
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0> mu;
  real<lower=0> tau;
  real theta[J];
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> alpha;
  real<lower=0> beta;
  real<lower=0> theta2[J];
  alpha <- (mu/tau)^2;
  beta <- mu/(tau^2);
  for (j in 1:J)
    theta2[j] <- theta[j]^2;
}
model {
  for(j in 1:J){
    theta2[j] ~ gamma(alpha, beta);
    increment_log_prob(log(fabs(2*theta[j])));
  }
  d ~ normal(theta, sigma);
}

And my data (I made all the distances positive, since sign is meaningless across units):

dat <- list(J = 16,
            d = c(0.551, 0.275, 0.307, 0.372, 0.165, 0.183, 0.656, 0.131, 0.632, 0.042, 0.003, 0.260, 0.488, 0.017, 0.130, 0.227),
            sigma = c(1.322, 0.179, 1.445, 0.565, 0.258, 1.231, 0.457, 0.648, 1.126, 0.590, 0.300, 0.351, 0.324, 0.394, 0.659, 0.441))

And my call to stan from R:

fit.squared <- stan(file = 'meta_squared.stan', data = dat, iter = 10000,
                    control = list("adapt_delta" = .9, "max_treedepth" = 10))

messages.subject: Gaussian Process modelling of an intercept+effect model with noisy replicates
messages.subject_clean: Gaussian Process modelling of an intercept+effect model with noisy replicates
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I've been trying to apply Gaussian Process models to data typical of my research domain for a while, and I think I've got it figured out now.

Here's a gist with R & stan code for a demonstration: https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/9ad22f38e53b575586ea238bf8388a2a

I've tried to comment both data-generation & model code thoroughly to walk you through the scenario.

The general idea is that the outcome Y is observed on a grid of values of X under two conditions. I want to model the possibly-non-linear functions of Y as a function of X in each condition, which I achieve by defining an "intercept" GP and "effect" GP and combining these to get two condition functions. Finally, because I have lots of observations per X per condition, I model these replicates as having random Gaussian deviations from their condition function.

The only issue that I seem to have left is that the model appears to have some numerical issues unless jitter is added to the GPs. That is, note that the model has a data variable called "fudge". If you set this to something very small, like 1e-7, the model takes a long time to sample but the resulting posteriors on both functions are nice and smooth. In contrast, if you set this to something larger like 1e-3, the model samples quickly but the posteriors on both functions are very noisy seeming.

I know that there is typically jitter added to a GP (usually called sigma), but it seemed unwise to do so in this case because I already add noise associated with the sampling of replicates from the GP. In the manual's section on GPs, the very last paragraph mentions notes that "A pure logistic Gaussian process regression would not include a noise term in the definition of the covariance matrix This can be implemented by simply removing the noise term(s) sigma_sq from the definition of Sigma.", so I presumed it would similarly be possible to eliminate it here. However, when I do so (by removing the fudge variable altogether), the model takes forever to sample for a given requested iteration count and has a very low ESS for the GP parameters.

Hence my workaround by adding fudge, but even with fudge included, there's still an annoying tradeoff between sampling speed and smoothness of the posterior. Any ideas on what might be done to avoid the tradeoff?

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.body_plain:
Andrew's also been asking us to start providing
lint-like warnings.

This is a good one --- our C++ compilers warn us when
we have an unused variable.

It's possible with the current Stan to C++ translation
pipeline, which produces an abstract syntax tree
intermediate representation.  That tree can be
walked and searched for variables, expression types,
functions, etc.

The complicated part is dealing with the Boost
variant types, which require a callback structure
rather than the usual kind of programming.  There
are lots of examples to follow.

- Bob

It's surprisingly tricky to do this right with string search.
There are quoted strings, substrings, operators and functions,
comments, declaration and use scope, and identifier
type.

Having said that, it'd be really great to build something
along the lines of Google's cpplint program, which we
use ourselves.  It's a Python program that runs over
C++ code looking for various kinds of coding problems.
You can get pretty far with string matching and also
detect other kinds of problems.

messages.subject: reproducible research with Docker, Rstan, and Gitlab CI
messages.subject_clean: reproducible research with Docker, Rstan, and Gitlab CI
messages.body_plain:
Hi Folks -

Just wanted to put a small something I've been working on out there to see what folks think about it.

This is a stab at making a template for a fully reproducible soup-to-nuts Stan-based project, that starts with input data and ends with a PDF containing figures and estimates derived from the model output. This repository contains all the code needed to re-generate a simple Stan example (fitting a 2-component finite mixture model) with a single command:

https://gitlab.com/jzelner/reproducible-stan

The ideas represented here are a crystallization of things that have been going on in a number of other projects of mine that rely on sensitive data and so can't be opened up in a way that is fully reproducible to anyone. There are three big reproducibility ideas in here, some newer than others, none of which are my own but instead represent a synthesis of some very powerful tools and ideas:

1) make: Everything is orchestrated using a Makefile that updates outputs as a function of their dependencies on each other. In some ways, this is the most powerful idea and a very old one.

2) Docker <https://www.docker.com/>: One of the challenges of reproducing any project (and Stan ones in particular for non-initiates) is having the relevant software installed locally to both run the Stan model and to do the requisite munging of model output. Docker provides a way to create a portable environment that can run everywhere without forcing users to go through the relatively complicated install process. For example, the example presented here relies on: R, assorted R packages (readr, ggplot2, dplyr, gridExtra), RStan, pandoc, TexLive, etc. The provided Docker image makes it easy to just download the whole environment and re-generate the model results without a complicated local install.

3) Continuous integration (CI): CI tools are commonly used in software engineering to make sure that small changes to a project don't break the whole thing. This project is hosted on Gitlab to take advantage of their easy-to-use and free Docker-based continuous integration service. This way, every time a commit is made to the repository, the Makefile is re-run and the model output (MCMC samples, figures and PDF writeup) are uploaded to the repository and are available for download.

More information (and all the code and output) are available in the repository. It's very much a work-in-progress and is meant more as a prod for more thought and development than anything else, so any feedback would be greatly appreciated!

-Jon

I'm repeating a question I posed here on Stack Overflow. <http://stackoverflow.com/questions/37493300/set-difference-in-stan>

I can't seem to figure out the best way to drop a column by index in Stan.

I have a matrix and I want to get all but one column of the matrix. For example, in R I would do the following:

    # Some matrix X
    X = matrix(nrow = 10, ncol = 4)

    # Approach 1 with setdiff
    X[, setdiff(1:ncol(X), 3)]

    # Direct approach in R
    X[, -3]

I cannot figure out the right way to do the same thing in Stan. Simple question, but any advice would help.

Thank you in advance, and sorry if this basic question has been answered elsewhere but I couldn't find it via google or the documentation.
Luke Sonnet

messages.body_plain:
There's no setdiff, and while you could build up
that set, you can also just do this:

  append_col(a[ , 1:2], a[ , 4:4])

to append two submatrices together by column.
In general, that's

   append_col(a[ , 1:(n-1)], a[ , (n+1):N])

but you have to watch out for n = 1 or n = N side
conditions.

- Bob

> > > > No, they are empirical percentiles estimated from the MCMC
> > > > draws.  In particular, the 2.5% and 97.5% estimates are very
> > > > very noisy and we do not recommend using then to estimate

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Should the sum-to-zero constrain added before sampling or after sampling?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Should the sum-to-zero constrain added before sampling or after sampling?
messages.body_plain:
1.  Yes, it's taking the gradients that makes things slow.
If you wind up doing something like inv(a) * b, it's better
to do a \ b and same for a * inv(b).

2.  That's a lot of questions about the underlying code.
The best bet's to use a Cholesky-based parameterization of
the covariance matrix (usually by scaling a Cholesky-based
parameteriation of the correlation matrix in our applications),
because then the solving required for the determinant is fast.

The other big speedup comes from group observations and/or
means into an array so that the matrix is only factored once.
This isn't possible if the covariance matrix varies with each
observation, but if it does, that's probably going to be a very
hard model to fit.

- Bob

> On May 26, 2016, at 9:51 PM, Jiang Du <jiang...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks for your advice. I've changed to use quad_form_diag when I was running the code.
>
> The way I want to build a covariance requires to inverse some matrix, say B. I even tried using its cholesky part L (LL'=B), and then inverse L. I think stan doesn't have the particular inverse for triangular matrices. But still, the inverse matrix is really slow and it takes more than a hour for 100 iterations. So I give up some "interpretation ability" of my current covariance matrix and find a way doing on the precision matrix, and the model gave me reliable results (a hour with 5000 iterations and convergence met).
>
> Here are some of my questions:
> 1. About the inverse. I did some Gibbs sampling involves the inverse of the covariance matrix as above in R, the speed is not that bad. Is that calculating the gradient making Stan not good at calculating the inverse? Since for a matrix not that huge (under 500*500), the inverse should be fast in C++ or R using the cholesky inverse method. (although  I  do try to avoid calculating the inverse every time when I'm programming, but this time the inverse is a must. )
>
> 2. When sampling from multivariate normal distribution, people usually use Cholesky decomposition to transfrom from a vector a N(0,1) random variables, which is fast. In stan, if u ~ multi_normal(0, Sigma), then which way is faster or better?
> 	•  One way is just specify as it is;
> 	• the other way is  u<-L*z where z~N(0,1), LL'=Sigma.
> 	• Or something like: u ~ multi_normal_cholesky(0, L) where LL'=Sigma.
> And when using multi_normal(0, Sigma), will it be expensive since Stan will calculate the inverse under the hood? Or, how does stan calculate the log density of multi_normal when given a covariance matrix, not precision one.
>
> Thanks,
>
> Jiang
>
>
> 在 2016年5月26日星期四 UTC-5下午2:33:24，Bob Carpenter写道：
> Also, you don't ever want to be computing inverses

> >
> > The whole idea about my model is jointly model two spatial variable, by explicitly define their cross covariance matrix (Not the precision, that's why the inverse can not be avoided). Suppose I have two spatial variables, y1 and y2, and let Y = c(y1, y2). Y is modeled by a Poisson regression framework, and using the log link, the
> > log_p = alpha + u + error;
> > for each variable, there will be a different alpha
> > u is the spatial effect for y1 and y2, follows a MVN(0, Sigma), where Sigma is a matrix of 4 blocks. The diagonal blocks are the usual covariance matrix for spatial CAR models, and the off-diagonal blocks are the matrix telling how the two spatial variables are correlated across maps.
> >
> > In order to identify alpha and u, I need to center u. That's why I followed Kyle Foreman's code.
> > Here is the scratch of the code:
> > data{
> >   int<lower=0> J1;#number of spatial regions for map 1
> >   int<lower=0> J2;#number of spatial regions for map 2
> >   int Y[J1+J2];#event counts for two maps, modeled in Poisson regression
> >   int pop[J1+J2];#corresponding population, offset
> >   matrix[J1, J1] W_1; #adgacency matrix for the first map
> >   matrix[J2, J2] W_2; #adgacency matrix for the first map
> >   matrix[J1, J1] D_1; #diagonal matrix with diag elemetns being number of neighbors
> >   matrix[J2, J2] D_2; #diagonal matrix with diag elemetns being number of neighbors
> >   matrix[J1, J2] Psi_12# a matrix to indicate how the regions in 2 maps are correlated
> > }
> > transformed data {
> >   # zeros for MVN prior
> >   vector[N] zeros;
> >   zeros <- rep_vector(0.0, N);
> > }
> > parameters{
> >   real<lower=0, upper=1> rho[2]; #strength of spatial correlation, for two maps
> >   vector[J1+J2] u; #spatial effect for two maps
> >   real<lower=-0.3,upper=0.3> gamma12;#correlation between two maps, restriced for positive definiteness
> >   vector[2] alpha; #intercept for each spatial map
> >   vector[J1+J2] epsilon;# standard Normal
> >   real<lower=0> sigma2; #variance for the error term in log mean of Poisson
> >   vector[2] delta;#variance compentent of the CAR model
> > }
> > transformed parameters{
> >   real<lower=0> sigma; #sqrt of sigma2
> >   sigma  <-  sqrt(sigma2);
> > }
> > model{
> >    matrix[J1, J1] B_1; #precision matrix for the 1st map
> >    matrix[J2, J2] B_2; #precision matrix for the 1st map
> >    matrix[J1+J2, J1+J2] Sigma;#covariance matrix for spatial effect;
> >    matrix[J1+J2, J1+J2] Sigma_full;#covariance matrix for spatial effect;
> >    vector[J1+J2] epsilon;# parameter for Poisson distribution in log scale
> >    vector[J1+J2] alpha_vec;#broadcast the intercept
> >    vector[J1+J2] delta_vec;#broadcast the variance compentent
> >    matrix[J1+J2, J1+J2] DELTA;#cange delta_vec to diag matrix
> >
> >    delta_vec[1:J1] <- rep_vector(delta[1], J1);
> >    delta_vec[(J1+1):J2] <- rep_vector(delta[2], J2);
> >    DELTA <- diag_matrix(delta_vec)
> >    alpha_vec[1:J1] <- rep_vector(alpha[1], J1);
> >    alpha_vec[(J1+1):J2] <- rep_vector(alpha[2], J2);
> >    B_1 <- D_1 - rho[1] * W_1;
> >    B_2 <- D_2 - rho[2] * W_2;
> >    #assign Sigma in block
> >    #Sigma = DELTA%*%
> >      #B_1_inv             gamma12*Psi_12
> >      #t(gamma12*Psi_12)   B_2_inv
> >    #%*%DELTA
> >    Sigma[1:J1, 1:J1] <- inverse_spd(B_1);
> >    Sigma[(J1+1):(J1+J2), (J1+1):(J1+J2)] <- inverse_spd(B_2);
> >    Sigma[1:J1, (J1+J2)] <- gamma12 * Psi_12;
> >    Sigma[(J1+1), 1:J1] <- (Sigma[1:J1, (J1+J2)])';
> >    Sigma_full <- DELTA*Sigma*DELTA;
> >    #prior for the spatial effect
> >    u ~ multi_normal(zeros, Sigma_full);
> >    epsilon ~ normal(0,1);
> >    log_p <- log(pop) + alpha_vec + u + sigma*epsilon;
> >    y ~ poisson_log(log_p);#likelihood
> > }
> >
> >
> > And based on your suggestions, is this the correct way doing the centering?

default uniform positive-constrained priors, then the posterior
is the same as the prior and is improper.  The mass is all in
the tail and the "mean" should diverge to +infinity.  So Stan's
doing roughly the right thing here, I think.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] use stan for time series clustering
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] use stan for time series clustering
messages.body_plain:
Yes, what you want to do is possible.  But you should
think about formulating the entire time series model,
then mixing that.  You're mixing at the time point level,
which probably isn't what you're after.

  p(y[n] | c, theta)  = SUM_k Categorical(k | c) Foo(y[n] | theta[k])

where each y[n] is a time series and theta[k] is a complete
set of parameters for mixture component k.

Then just do that with log_sum_exp() on the log scale.

   log p(y[n] | c, theta)
    = LOG_SUM_EXP_k log Categorical(k | c) + log Foo(y[n] | theta[k])

- Bob

> On May 29, 2016, at 6:06 PM, Bin Han <danie...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I am trying to use stan to do a time series clustering, using mixture model kind of idea. An example usage is given economic metric time series for a set of states in US, cluster the states based on similarity of their time series. The idea is having a mixture of AR(p) model for each cluster. The prior for cluster can dirichlet, and the prior for AR parameter phi can be multivariate normal.
>
> The model is following:
>
> N: # of states,
> T: # of ts data points,
> K: # of clusters,
> p: parameter for AR(p),
> cluster ~ dirichlet, (for each state n)
> phi ~ multi_normal(psi0, omega0), (for each cluster k )
>
> likelihood: y_{n, t} ~ product_over_k (normal(mu_k, sigma_k) * prob(cluster_{n, k})), (this is kinda like the soft k mean likelihood)
>
> where mu = phi_{k, 1} + phi_{k, 2} * y_{n, t-1} + ... phi_{k, p+1} * y_{n, t-p},
> and sigma ~ gamma(a0, b0).
>
> The stan code is as follows:
>
> data {
>   int K; int P; int N; int T;  # K clusters, P auto-reg, N items, T ts data points
>   vector[T] y[N];  # ts data
>   vector[P + 1] psi0[K];  # prior for psi
>   vector<lower=0>[K] e0;  # prior for cluster
> }
>
> parameters {
>   vector[P + 1] psi[K];
>   real<lower=0> sigma[K];  # std for data
>   simplex[K] c[N];
> }
>
> model {
>   real ps[K];
>
>   for (n in 1:N){
>     for (t in (P + 1):T){
>       for (k in 1:K) {
>         ps[k] <- log(c[n, k]) + normal_log(y[n, t], psi[k, 1] + dot_product(psi[k, 2:(P + 1)], y[n, (t - 1):(t - P)]), sigma[k]);
>       }
>       increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));
>     }
>   }
>
>   sigma ~ gamma(2, 0.5);
>   for (k in 1:K)
>     psi[k] ~ normal(psi0[k], 100);
>   for (n in 1:N)

> }

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] reproducible research with Docker, Rstan, and Gitlab CI
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] reproducible research with Docker, Rstan, and Gitlab CI
messages.body_plain:
Has anyone tried running this on Windows?

How big are the docker images?  How big would it be without
R, LaTeX, etc?  I'm wondering how feasible it would be to
distribute a working Stan system this way and then communicate
with it via protocol buffers.  Then we could have lightweight
command-line, R, and Python wrappers.

- Bob

> On May 27, 2016, at 3:00 PM, Jon Zelner <jze...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Folks -
>
> Just wanted to put a small something I've been working on out there to see what folks think about it.
>
> This is a stab at making a template for a fully reproducible soup-to-nuts Stan-based project, that starts with input data and ends with a PDF containing figures and estimates derived from the model output. This repository contains all the code needed to re-generate a simple Stan example (fitting a 2-component finite mixture model) with a single command:
>
> https://gitlab.com/jzelner/reproducible-stan
>
> The ideas represented here are a crystallization of things that have been going on in a number of other projects of mine that rely on sensitive data and so can't be opened up in a way that is fully reproducible to anyone. There are three big reproducibility ideas in here, some newer than others, none of which are my own but instead represent a synthesis of some very powerful tools and ideas:
>
> 1) make: Everything is orchestrated using a Makefile that updates outputs as a function of their dependencies on each other. In some ways, this is the most powerful idea and a very old one.
>
> 2) Docker: One of the challenges of reproducing any project (and Stan ones in particular for non-initiates) is having the relevant software installed locally to both run the Stan model and to do the requisite munging of model output. Docker provides a way to create a portable environment that can run everywhere without forcing users to go through the relatively complicated install process. For example, the example presented here relies on: R, assorted R packages (readr, ggplot2, dplyr, gridExtra), RStan, pandoc, TexLive, etc. The provided Docker image makes it easy to just download the whole environment and re-generate the model results without a complicated local install.
>
> 3) Continuous integration (CI): CI tools are commonly used in software engineering to make sure that small changes to a project don't break the whole thing. This project is hosted on Gitlab to take advantage of their easy-to-use and free Docker-based continuous integration service. This way, every time a commit is made to the repository, the Makefile is re-run and the model output (MCMC samples, figures and PDF writeup) are uploaded to the repository and are available for download.
>
> More information (and all the code and output) are available in the repository. It's very much a work-in-progress and is meant more as a prod for more thought and development than anything else, so any feedback would be greatly appreciated!
>
> -Jon
>

I have made a few attempts but I think I'm missing something crucial.

Below is my Stan code:

data {
    // data size
    int<lower=1> n_polls;
    int<lower=1> n_span;
    int<lower=1> n_houses;

    // poll data
    real<lower=0,upper=1> y[n_polls];
    real<lower=0> prec[n_polls];
    int<lower=1> houses[n_polls];
    int<lower=1> day[n_polls];
}
parameters {
    real<lower=0,upper=1> hidden_voting_intention[n_span];
    real<lower=0,upper=1> houseEffect[n_houses];
    real<lower=0,upper=0.01> sigma;
}
model{
    // -- temporal model
    sigma ~ uniform(0, 0.01);
    hidden_voting_intention[1] ~ normal(0.5363, 0.001);
    hidden_voting_intention[946] ~ normal(0.4902, 0.001);
    hidden_voting_intention[2080] ~ normal(0.5095, 0.001);
    hidden_voting_intention[3144] ~ normal(0.5274, 0.001);
    hidden_voting_intention[4285] ~ normal(0.473, 0.001);
    hidden_voting_intention[5280] ~ normal(0.4988, 0.001);
    hidden_voting_intention[6399] ~ normal(0.5349, 0.001);
    for(i in 2:n_span) {
        hidden_voting_intention[i] ~ normal(hidden_voting_intention[i-1], sigma);
    }

    // -- observational model
    for(poll in 1:n_polls) {
        y[poll] ~ normal(houseEffect[houses[poll]] + hidden_voting_intention[day[poll]], prec[poll]);
    }
}

I am not entirely sure how to anchor the voting intention to the election results in the Stan framework. I have the election results for 7 dates and I'm not entirely sure on the best way to incorporate them into the model given I cannot (or have failed to) create hidden_voting_intention as data with the election results and missing data points to be estimated.

Here is my R code:
##### Luke Mansillo - Pooling the Polls

coo <- list()

> There's an HMM example in the manual, but that involves
> discrete state spaces that get marginalized out.
> Your model has only continuous parameters (I think --- the
> BUGS/JAGS models don't declare variable types), so you
> don't need to do that (though in some cases, if everything's
> conjugate, you can marginalize out the continuous states,
> as in Kalman filters).
>
> We don't recommend interval priors like this, and they
> behave very differently in BUGS/JAGS than Stan for scale

>

> scale sigma is going to have small variation.  We recommend (see

> >
> > ## initial values for priors
> >
> > initfunc <- function(){

> >              NA) ## missing chain point
> >   sigma <- runif(n=1,0,.01)  ## uniform prior on standard deviation
> >   list(house=house, ## parameter - house effect

> > }
> >
> > ## send to WinBUGS

> > houseend <- length(foo$alpha)+6

> >
> > ## read BUGS output back into R

> > alpha <- read.bugs(daily)
> > house <- alpha[,housestart:houseend]
> > sigma <- alpha[,sigmaend]
> > alpha <- alpha[,1:periodend]
> >
> > alpha.bar <- apply(as.matrix(alpha),2,mean)
> > alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci> <- apply(as.matrix(alpha),2,quantile,c(.025,.975))
> >
> > ## estimates
> >
> > alpha.bar <- c(.5363,as.matrix(alpha.bar)[1:944],.4902,as.matrix(alpha.bar)[945:2077],.5095,as.matrix(alpha.bar)[2078:3140],.5274,as.matrix(alpha.bar)[3141:4280],.4730,as.matrix(alpha.bar)[4281:5280],.4988,as.matrix(alpha.bar)[5281:6392],.5349,as.matrix(alpha.bar)[6393:length(alpha.bar)])
> > alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci> <- t(matrix(c(.5363,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[1,1:944],.4902,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[1,945:2077],.5095,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[1,2078:3140],.5274,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[1,3141:4280],.4730,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[1,4281:5280],.4988,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[1,5281:6392],.5349,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[1,6393:length(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)],
> >                        .5363,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[2,1:944],.4902,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[2,945:2077],.5095,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[2,2078:3140],.5274,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[2,3141:4280],.4730,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[2,4281:5280],.4988,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[2,5281:6392],.5349,as.matrix(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)[2,6393:length(alpha.ci <http://alpha.ci>)]),nrow=length(alpha.bar),ncol=2))

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] reproducible research with Docker, Rstan, and Gitlab CI
messages.body_plain:
Docker support for Windows is new-ish.
https://docs.docker.com/engine/installation/windows/

One issue with docker is that it runs as a privileged user by default.
By contrast, you can use a C++ compiler (and Stan) without being a
privileged user.

A

On 05/29, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Has anyone tried running this on Windows?
>
> How big are the docker images?  How big would it be without
> R, LaTeX, etc?  I'm wondering how feasible it would be to
> distribute a working Stan system this way and then communicate
> with it via protocol buffers.  Then we could have lightweight
> command-line, R, and Python wrappers.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On May 27, 2016, at 3:00 PM, Jon Zelner <jze...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Folks -
> >
> > Just wanted to put a small something I've been working on out there to see what folks think about it.
> >
> > This is a stab at making a template for a fully reproducible soup-to-nuts Stan-based project, that starts with input data and ends with a PDF containing figures and estimates derived from the model output. This repository contains all the code needed to re-generate a simple Stan example (fitting a 2-component finite mixture model) with a single command:
> >
> > https://gitlab.com/jzelner/reproducible-stan
> >
> > The ideas represented here are a crystallization of things that have been going on in a number of other projects of mine that rely on sensitive data and so can't be opened up in a way that is fully reproducible to anyone. There are three big reproducibility ideas in here, some newer than others, none of which are my own but instead represent a synthesis of some very powerful tools and ideas:
> >
> > 1) make: Everything is orchestrated using a Makefile that updates outputs as a function of their dependencies on each other. In some ways, this is the most powerful idea and a very old one.
> >
> > 2) Docker: One of the challenges of reproducing any project (and Stan ones in particular for non-initiates) is having the relevant software installed locally to both run the Stan model and to do the requisite munging of model output. Docker provides a way to create a portable environment that can run everywhere without forcing users to go through the relatively complicated install process. For example, the example presented here relies on: R, assorted R packages (readr, ggplot2, dplyr, gridExtra), RStan, pandoc, TexLive, etc. The provided Docker image makes it easy to just download the whole environment and re-generate the model results without a complicated local install.
> >
> > 3) Continuous integration (CI): CI tools are commonly used in software engineering to make sure that small changes to a project don't break the whole thing. This project is hosted on Gitlab to take advantage of their easy-to-use and free Docker-based continuous integration service. This way, every time a commit is made to the repository, the Makefile is re-run and the model output (MCMC samples, figures and PDF writeup) are uploaded to the repository and are available for download.
> >
> > More information (and all the code and output) are available in the repository. It's very much a work-in-progress and is meant more as a prod for more thought and development than anything else, so any feedback would be greatly appreciated!
> >
> > -Jon
